passages.title: The Book sent down on a blessed night
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are Allah's own testimony about the Qur'an: where it came from, when it came down, why it was sent, and Who sent it. The thread holding them together is a single unbroken movement of witness — an oath sworn by the Book (ayah 2), the night of its descent (ayah 3), what else is settled on that night (ayat 4–5), the motive behind the whole affair (ayah 6), and finally the identity of the Sender, named with rising clarity until the passage closes on pure tawhid (ayat 7–8).

## Ayat 1–2: the letters, and an oath sworn by the Book

The surah opens with **Ḥā-Mīm**, then immediately: *wa'l-kitābi'l-mubīn* — "By the clear Book!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this verse refers to the Holy Qur'an, and that in it Allah swears an oath by the magnificent Qur'an. Maʿārif adds that a similar oath was taken, in exactly the same words, at the commencement of Surah Az-Zukhruf (chapter 43), where the oath-phrase has been fully discussed.

Consider what an oath is for. A person swears to make a listener take him seriously. Allah swears by the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir renders *al-kitāb al-mubīn* as "the manifest Book that makes things clear" — that rendering holds two senses at once: the Book is itself manifest, and it makes things clear. So the guarantee and the thing guaranteed are the same Book. And Maʿārif states what the oath is *for*: Allah swears by the magnificent Qur'an to state that it was revealed in a blessed and auspicious night, the purpose of which is to awaken unmindful human beings from their deep slumber. That is worth pausing on: the passage is not primarily informing people who are curious. It is waking people who are asleep.

## A glimpse from the Sīrah: the surah the Prophet ﷺ concealed

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this surah with a striking incident. In *Musnad Al-Bazzar*, it is recorded from Abu At-Tufayl ʿAmir bin Wathilah, from Zayd bin Harithah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ibn Sayyad, "I am concealing something, what is it?" — and what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was concealing from him was Surat Ad-Dukhan. Ibn Sayyad said: "It is *Ad-Dukh*." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ replied, "Be off with you! Whatever Allah wills happens."

Set that fragment — *Ad-Dukh* — beside ayah 2's *al-kitāb al-mubīn*. One is a broken half-word that catches at the edge of the name and cannot reach it; the other is a Book that is manifest and makes things clear. The contrast frames everything that follows.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also opens with the merit of this surah, reporting two traditions: Sayyidna Abu Hurairah reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whoever recites Surah Dukhan on Friday night, his sins will have been forgiven by the morning; and Sayyidna Umamah narrates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that anyone who recites Surah Dukhan on Friday, in the night or in the day, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise. Maʿārif transmits both from Qurtubi on the authority of Thalabi; no hadith collection is named for them in our sources, so they are best received exactly as Maʿārif passes them on.

## Ayah 3: "We sent it down on a blessed night"

**Which night?** Ibn Kathir states it plainly: Allah tells us that He revealed the Magnificent Qur'an on a blessed night, Laylatul-Qadr, the Night of Decree — citing His own words elsewhere, *"Verily, We have sent it down in the Night of Al-Qadr"* (97:1), and that this was in the month of Ramadan, *"The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an"* (2:185). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees, saying this is the position of the majority of the commentators: the blessed night is Laylatul-Qadr, the Night of Power, which occurs in the last ten nights of Ramadan, and during it Allah sends down countless blessings for His servants. The Qur'an is thus its own commentary here — 97:1 and 2:185 together name the night and the month.

**Two descents, not one.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unlocks something that puzzles many readers. The Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ gradually over a period of twenty-three years — so how can a single night be *the* night of its revelation? The answer Maʿārif gives: to say the Qur'an was revealed on the Night of Power means it was revealed in its entirety from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfūz*) to the lowest Firmament in one night of the month of Ramadan, while its delivery to the Prophet ﷺ then unfolded gradually across those twenty-three years. Maʿārif adds a second view held by some scholars: that the instalment of the Qur'an destined to be revealed in a given year used to be sent down on the Night of Power from the Preserved Tablet to the Firmament of the Earth (both reported via Qurtubi).

**Ramadan and the earlier scriptures.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits a report that this month has always been revelation's season: it is narrated in a tradition of the Prophet ﷺ that all Prophets, from the inception of man till the end, received their respective Books in the month of Ramadan on different dates. Sayyidna Qatadah reports on the authority of Sayyidna Wathilah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) received his Scriptures on the 1st of Ramadan, the Torah was revealed on the 6th, the Zabur on the 12th, the Injil on the 18th, and the Holy Qur'an on the night of the 24th, that is, the 25th of Ramadan (Qurtubi). No hadith collection is named for this report in the sources before us, so take it as Maʿārif transmits it, through Qurtubi.

**"Verily, We are ever warning."** The second half of ayah 3 supplies the reason. Ibn Kathir explains it as: telling them what is good for them and what is harmful for them, according to the Sharīʿah, *so that the proof of Allah may be established against His servants*. Note the moral shape of that. Revelation is first a warning and a kindness — you are told before you are held to account. Nobody arrives on the Day of Judgement able to say the terms were hidden.

## Ayat 4–5: the night when the year is handed over

**"Therein is decreed every matter, ḥakīm."** Ibn Kathir explains what this decreeing actually is: on Laylatul-Qadr, the decrees are transferred from *al-Lawh al-Mahfūz*, the Preserved Tablet, to the angelic scribes, who write down the decrees of the coming year, including life span, provision, and what will happen until the end of the year. He records this from Ibn ʿUmar, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ad-Dahhak and others among the Salaf.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same picture with its own line of authorities: Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas said this ayah refers to the Night of Power, in which the Qur'an was revealed, and that in it all matters are decreed to happen from the present Night of Power to the next, relating to all creation, their births, their deaths, their provisions and other details. Other leading authorities on tafsir — Sayyidna Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid and others — concur with him. Mahdawi says that all matters decreed by Allah are, on this night, transferred to the angelic scribes who record the decrees of the coming year.

**Does this mean Allah decides that night?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the obvious question head-on, and the answer matters for correct belief. Other texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah bear testimony to the fact that Allah had decreed all matters in pre-eternity (*azal*), even before the creation of man. Therefore the statement that a person's destiny is decreed on this night simply means that the decrees for the whole year are *handed over*, that night, to the relevant angels for implementation (Qurtubi). Nothing new enters Allah's knowledge. What happens is a disclosure and a deployment, not a decision being reached.

**Ḥakīm.** Ibn Kathir gives its force here precisely: *ḥakīm* means decided or confirmed, which cannot be changed or altered. So the year's decree is not a draft. It is settled and it is fixed.

**"As a command from Us."** Ibn Kathir: everything that happens and is decreed by Allah, and the revelation that He sends down — it all happens by His command, by His leave and with His knowledge. One sovereign will stands behind both the Book descending and the year unfolding; they are two motions of a single command.

**"Verily, We are ever sending."** Ibn Kathir explains: sending to mankind Messengers who will recite to them the clear signs of Allah — and he adds a phrase worth noticing, that *the need for this was urgent*. The continuous sense, "ever sending," presents the sending of Messengers as a standing practice of divine mercy rather than a one-off event.

## The blessed night: where scholars differed

Because this passage is often quoted in discussions of mid-Shaʿban, it is worth setting out the disagreement carefully and attributing each side, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does.

Some other scholars of tafsir, among them ʿIkrimah, read *laylah mubārakah* as *laylat-ul-barā'ah*, the Night of Immunity — the 15th night of Shaʿban. Maʿārif notes the reason this reading arose: some versions of the tradition state that births, deaths and sustenance are decreed on that night.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not accept this reading of *this* ayah, and gives its reasons: here the revelation of the Qur'an is mentioned first, and its revelation in the month of Ramadan is confirmed by the clear texts of the Qur'an — 2:185 and 97:1. In the presence of such clear texts, it cannot be accepted without strong evidence that the Qur'an was revealed on the Night of Immunity.

As for the reports about mid-Shaʿban themselves, Maʿārif relays the assessments of several authorities:

- **Ibn Kathir** says this tradition is *mursal* — a technical grading in the science of hadith, which our sources use here without defining it — and that such a tradition cannot be reliable in the presence of clear, express texts.
- **Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn ʿArabi** asserts that no authentic tradition relating to mid-Shaʿban is available showing that sustenance, births and deaths are determined and decreed on that night, and he further rejects the idea that there is any reliable tradition on the merit of this night.
- **Ruh-ul-Maʿani** cites a tradition — *without a chain of transmitters* — narrated by Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas, in which he says that sustenance, life and death are determined on the mid-Shaʿban night, and that on the Night of Power the decrees are handed over to the angels. Maʿārif notes that if this tradition were confirmed, the two interpretations could be reconciled; otherwise the express words of the Qur'an and the authentic traditions point to the Night of Power.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own summing-up is balanced, and it is worth keeping its balance rather than sharpening it: the merit of mid-Shaʿban is a separate issue from this ayah; some traditions do speak about it, but they are weak, which is why Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn ʿArabi denied any merit for the night. Their chains of transmission are all weak, though it may be suggested that if the various ways of transmission are put together they gain strength — and many great scholars have accepted them, since there is room to act upon weak traditions relating to meritorious actions. Maʿārif ends where an honest scholar ends: *Allah knows best.*

The takeaway is twofold. On the meaning of *this* passage, our sources are firm: the blessed night here is the Night of Power in Ramadan. On the wider question of mid-Shaʿban's merit, the scholars our sources name genuinely differed, and Maʿārif leaves the matter open.

## Ayah 6: why any of it happened

*"As a mercy from your Lord."* This is the hinge of the passage. Every element named so far — the Book, the night, the decree, the Messengers — is now given a single motive: mercy. And it is not abstract mercy but *mercy from your Lord* — addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and through him to everyone who receives the Book. The warning of ayah 3 and the mercy of ayah 6 are the same act described from two sides.

*"Verily, He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower"* — *as-Samīʿ, al-ʿAlīm*. These are the names by which Allah describes Himself at the close of this ayah, and their placement is pointed: the One who decrees your year is the One who hears and the One who knows. The decree is not blind machinery. It issues from Him.

## Ayat 7–8: the Sender identified

Ibn Kathir draws ayat 6 and 7 together in one stroke: *the One Who sent down the Qur'an is the Lord, Creator and Sovereign of the heavens and the earth and everything in between them.* The argument is quietly overwhelming. If the Book comes from the One who owns and sustains the entire cosmos, then to shrug at the Book is to misjudge your own position within it.

Ayah 7 closes with a condition that stings: **"if you (but) have a faith with certainty"** — *in kuntum mūqinīn*. It is not that Allah's lordship depends on your certainty; it is that the whole preceding argument only lands on someone willing to be certain. To the person who will not commit, these words pass by as information. To the one who receives them with certainty, they reorganise a life.

Then ayah 8 removes every remaining alternative: **"Lā ilāha illā Huwa. He gives life and causes death — your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers."** Ibn Kathir notes that this is like Allah's words: *"Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah — to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Lā ilāha illā Huwa. He gives life and causes death..."* (7:158). The same three moves appear in both places: a universal address, sovereignty over the heavens and the earth, then *lā ilāha illā Huwa* with life and death in His hand alone.

Two details in ayah 8 deserve attention. First, *He gives life and causes death* is precisely the subject matter of the decree in ayah 4 as Ibn Kathir describes it — life span and provision. The One who apportions the year is the One who owns life itself. Second, the ayah does not stop at *your Lord*: it says *and the Lord of your forefathers*. His lordship is not a claim made only over the living generation; the generations that came before stood under the same Lord.

## Living it

**Take the night seriously.** The sources give a concrete practice, not a mood: the last ten nights of Ramadan contain a night on which the year's decree — life span, provision, what will happen until the end of the year — is handed to the angels. A believer who knows this does not let those nights pass unattended.

**Hold the decree and the du'a together.** Ayah 4, as Ibn Kathir reads it, says every matter is decided and confirmed, not to be changed or altered; ayah 6 says the One behind it is *as-Samīʿ*, the All-Hearer. The believer's posture is therefore neither fatalism nor anxiety: submit to what is written, and keep asking the One who hears.

**Let the warning do its work.** Ibn Kathir says the warning came so that the proof of Allah may be established against His servants. Having read this, you now stand inside that proof. The Book was described as *mubīn* — manifest, and making things clear — which means the remaining question is never whether the message was plain, only what you do with it.

**Read it as mercy.** Ayah 6 names the motive. If reading the Qur'an ever feels like being audited, this ayah corrects the frame: it was sent as mercy from your Lord, by the One who hears and knows, and who is Lord of you and of those who came before you.

passages.title: The day of smoke, and their plea for relief
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath.** The certain truth had reached the idolaters of Makkah, and they treated it as something to play with. Ayat 9–12 answer that posture: a day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke that covers the people, and the very men who played crying out to their Lord to lift it, promising that this time they will believe. What binds the four ayat into one unit is a single movement — from *amusement* (ayah 9) to *anguish* (ayah 12).

## Ayah 9 — doubt that is played with

*Bal hum fī shakkin yalʿabūn* — "In fact, they are in doubt, amusing themselves."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is direct: "these idolaters are playing about in doubt, i.e., the certain truth has come to them, but they doubt it and do not believe in it."

Read that carefully. The problem he identifies is not that the evidence failed to arrive. The certain truth *came to them*. What they did with it was doubt it, disbelieve it, and treat it as a plaything. Ibn Kathir titles this whole passage "Alarming the Idolators with News of the Day when the Sky will bring forth a visible Smoke" — the warning that follows is the answer to that posture.

## Ayah 10 — "Wait then, for the day"

*Fa-rtaqib yawma taʾtī s-samāʾu bi-dukhānin mubīn* — "Wait then, O Prophet, for the day when the sky will bring forth a visible smoke."

Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah with a single line about its function: "Then Allah says, warning and threatening them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way — the ayah "embodies a prophecy," and the Prophet ﷺ "was asked to watch for the Day when the sky will bring forth a manifest smoke covering the people."

The key word is *mubīn*. Ibn Kathir explains it as "clearly visible, such that all people will see it." That single adjective becomes the hinge of the whole scholarly discussion below.

## Which smoke is this? Three views

This is the question the commentators spend most of their energy on. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets it out plainly: "There are three opinions recorded about this from the Companions and their pupils."

### 1. A sign of the Hour, still awaited

Held by Sayyidnā al-Murtaḍā, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Hurayrah, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn Abī Mulaykah and others, may Allah be pleased with them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the view "is recorded traceably on the authority of" Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Hudhayfah ibn Usayd al-Ghifārī.

Muslim records in his *Sahih* — and Ibn Kathir notes it was "recorded only by Muslim" — that Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifārī said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked out upon us from a room while we were discussing the Hour," and he ﷺ said: **"The Hour will not come until you see ten signs: the rising of the sun from the west; the smoke; the beast; the emergence of Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj; the appearance of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam; the Dajjāl; three cases of the earth collapsing — one in the east, one in the west, and one in the Arabian Peninsula; and a fire which will emerge from the bottom of Aden and will drive the people — or gather the people — stopping with them when they stop to sleep at night or rest during the day."** The smoke stands there in a list of things plainly still ahead.

A second incident points the same way. In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said to Ibn Ṣayyād, "I am concealing something for you," and Ibn Ṣayyād answered, "It is *ad-Dukh*." The Prophet ﷺ replied, "Be off with you! You cannot get further than your rank." What he ﷺ had concealed was this very ayah — *fa-rtaqib yawma taʾtī s-samāʾu bi-dukhānin mubīn*. Ibn Kathir explains that Ibn Ṣayyād was a fortune-teller who heard things through the jinn, whose speech is unclear, so all he could produce was the broken syllable "*ad-Dukh*" for *ad-Dukhān*. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sure that the source of his information was the shayāṭīn, he dismissed him. Ibn Kathir draws the inference in one sentence: "This indicates that the smoke is yet to appear."

Ibn Jarīr also records, on the authority of Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I warn you against three things: one, the smoke, which will only cause cold in a believer, but will permeate the entire body of an unbeliever so much so that it will ooze out from every pore and minute hole of the skin; the second thing is the beast; the third thing will be Dajjāl." Having cited it, Ibn Kathir said: "This chain of transmitters is good."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes further that Ibn Kathir cites a narration on the same subject through Ibn Abī Ḥātim on the authority of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and another through Ibn Abī Ḥātim from al-Murtaḍā to the effect that "this prophecy has not yet been fulfilled," with the same description of the smoke; and that Ibn Jarīr cites a narration on the same subject from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās.

### 2. It has already happened — Ibn Masʿūd's reading

The other major view belongs to ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, and the way it reaches us is itself one of the most instructive stories in this sūrah.

Masrūq narrated: "We entered the Masjid — the Masjid of Kūfah at the gates of Kindah — and a man was reciting to his companions, *the Day when the sky will bring forth a visible smoke*. He asked them, 'Do you know what that is?' That is the smoke that will come on the Day of Resurrection. It will take away the hearing and sight of the hypocrites, but for the believers it will be like having a cold."

Masrūq continues: "We came to Ibn Masʿūd and told him about that. He was lying down, and he sat up with a start" — the detail is vivid — "and said, 'Allah said to your Prophet ﷺ: *Say: "No wage do I ask of you for this, nor am I one of the pretenders"* (38:86). And it is part of knowledge that when a man does not know something, he should say, "Allah knows best."'"

Before he gives his own view, he teaches the manners of not pretending. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders his point on 38:86 this way: the verse "proves that it is also a part of knowledge that when a man does not know something, he should say frankly that he does not know and that the correct knowledge is with Allah — and he should not pretend that he knows it."

Then he gave the history. "I will tell you a Hadith about that. When the Quraysh did not respond to Islam and they grew stubborn, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked Allah against them that they would have years like the years of drought and famine of Yūsuf. They became so exhausted and hungry that they ate bones and dead meat. They looked at the sky, but they saw nothing but smoke." Another report puts it more precisely: "A man would look at the sky and he would see nothing between him and the sky except a smoky haze, because of his exhaustion." On this reading, the "smoke" is the grey blur of starvation — a man looking up for rain-clouds and seeing only a haze produced by his own hunger.

The account continues into the ayat just past our passage, which is how Ibn Masʿūd's argument is completed: a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah! Pray to Allah to send rain to Muḍar, for they are dying." He ﷺ prayed for rain, and rain came. Then *Verily, We shall remove the torment for a while. Verily, you will revert* (44:15) was revealed. Ibn Masʿūd said: "Do you think that the torment will be removed for them on the Day of Resurrection? When they were granted ease, they reverted to their former state." Then came *On the Day when We shall strike you with the great Baṭshah. Verily, We will exact retribution* (44:16), which he said "means the day of Badr."

He summed it up: **"Five things have come to pass: the smoke, the defeat of the Romans, the splitting of the moon, the Baṭshah, and the torment."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists the same five and gives the fifth under the name *lizām*, identifying each in turn: the "smoke" is the drought and famine of Makkah; the Romans is the prophecy of *and they, after their defeat, will be victorious* (30:3); the moon is the miracle of *the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split asunder* (54:1); the seizure is what the pagan Quraysh met at Badr; and the *lizām* refers to *the punishment will be inseparable from you* (25:77) — meaning, as Maʿārif puts it, that "the unbelievers' persistent denial of the truth will inevitably cause them torment."

This report was narrated in the Two Sahihs. It was also recorded by Imām Aḥmad in his *Musnad*, by at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī in their books of Tafsir, and by Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim with a number of chains of narration. A number of the Salaf — Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī — concurred with Ibn Masʿūd that the smoke had already happened, and this was Ibn Jarīr's view too.

### 3. The dust of the Conquest

A third view, from ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān al-Aʿraj and others, takes the "smoke" as the dust stirred up to the sky, covering the firmament of Makkah on the day of the Conquest of Makkah (Qurṭubī). Ibn Kathir dismisses it in strong terms: "This view is *gharīb* (unfamiliar), in fact *munkar*" — that is, against the authentic reports.

### Where the commentators land

The first two views are the ones with real weight; as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, they "are confirmed by authentic Traditions." Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī supports the second; Tafsīr Bayān ul-Qurʼān prefers it; "it would appear that Ibn Kathir and Qurṭubī prefer the first. Allah knows best."

Ibn Kathir's reason is drawn from the wording itself, and it is worth following closely. He grants that on Ibn Masʿūd's interpretation the smoke "was a vision which they saw because of their intense hunger and exhaustion," and that *yaghshā n-nās* means "it covered them and overwhelmed them." Then comes his objection: **"But if it was only an illusion which happened to the idolators of Makkah, Allah would not have said 'covering mankind.'"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands the same point: the wordings "expressly refer to the distinctive smoke that would be brought forth in the open and clear sky, enshrouding all the people. But in this interpretation, there is neither visible smoke in the sky nor is it enveloping the people."

He weighs the transmitted evidence the same way. The chain is "authentic up to Ibn ʿAbbās, the scholar of the Ummah, interpreter of the Qurʼān"; add the views of the Companions and their pupils who agreed with him, "together with prophetic Traditions — some being sahih and others hasan," and the case that the smoke is one of the awaited portents of the Hour is strong, "especially since the apparent wordings of the Qurʼān bear evidence to this fact." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the methodological point plainly: this interpretation is preferable "because this is based on Prophetic ahadith, while the other interpretation is based merely on a saying of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd."

There is even a way of holding both. Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī cites, from ʿAllāmah Saffārīnī's *al-Buḥūr az-Zākhirah*, a narration that there are **two** smokes produced at two different times: "One, in fact, has already occurred on the occasion of the famine of Makkah and the other is still going to be produced. The second smoke will fill the atmosphere between the heaven and the earth. A believer will feel it like having a cold but it will tear through all the pores of an unbeliever." If that narration could be confirmed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, "there will remain no conflict between the Tafsir of Ibn Masʿūd and the express wordings of the Qurʼān and the Prophetic ahadith." But the author of Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī himself expressed suspicion about its authenticity — so it stands as a possible reconciliation, not a settled conclusion. Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.

## Ayah 11 — "covering the people; this is a painful torment"

*Yaghshā n-nās* — Ibn Kathir glosses it: "it covered them and overwhelmed them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "that will envelop people," and reads the wording as showing "that the smoke had enveloped all the people." No gap is left; nowhere the smoke does not reach.

The second half — *hādhā ʿadhābun alīm*, "this is a painful torment" — is not narration but speech. Ibn Kathir gives two possibilities: it is said to them "by way of rebuke," as in *The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing. This is the Fire which you used to deny* (52:13–14); "or some of them will say that to others." Either way, the sentence carries a bitter echo of ayah 9. They played about a warning of torment; now the word *torment* is in their own mouths.

## Ayah 12 — the prayer that is not repentance

*Rabbanā ikshif ʿannā l-ʿadhāba innā muʾminūn* — "Our Lord! Remove the torment from us; truly we shall become believers."

Look at what they get right. They address Allah as *Rabbanā*, our Lord. Ibn Kathir puts the mechanism simply: "when the disbelievers witness the punishment of Allah, they will ask for it to be taken away from them." Under that smoke, no one is amusing himself any more.

But the Qurʼān presents this cry as a known pattern rather than a turning point. Ibn Kathir sets it beside two other passages: *If you could but see when they will be held over the Fire! They will say: "Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers!"* (6:27); and *And warn mankind of the Day when the torment will come unto them; then the wrongdoers will say: "Our Lord! Respite us for a little while, we will answer Your Call and follow the Messengers!"* (14:44). The same words come out every time.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the whole sequence out as a chain of prophecies contained in these ayat: "First, the appearance of smoke on the sky and enveloping all the people. Second, that the pagans will not be able to bear the torment, so they will pray to Allah for its removal promising that they will believe. Third, they will go back on their words and break their promise." Our ayah is the second link — and the third is already written into it.

### Looking just past our four ayat

The ayat immediately following (44:13–16) are outside this passage, but the commentators treat them together with it, and two points from there bear directly on how ayah 12 is read.

Ibn Kathir places *How can there be for them an admonition, when a Messenger explaining things clearly has already come to them* (44:13) right after the cry, and paraphrases: what further admonition do they need, when a Messenger came to them with a clear message and warning, and despite that they turned away from him, opposed him and rejected him? He compares *On that Day will man remember, but how will that remembrance then avail him?* (89:23), and *they will say, "We do believe now"; but how could they receive it from a place so far off* (34:51–52).

And on *Verily, We shall remove the torment for a while. Verily, you will revert* (44:15), Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: "if We were to remove the torment from you for a while, and send you back to the world, you would go back to your former state of disbelief and denial" — as in *And though We had mercy on them and removed the distress which is on them, still they would obstinately persist in their transgression* (23:75), and *if they were returned, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden — and indeed they are liars* (6:28). Their *innā muʾminūn* is not only a promise they break; the Qurʼān names them liars in making it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difficulty here, and it is fair to name it: if the smoke belongs to the Hour, how can 44:15 speak of removing the punishment for a while, when on the Day of Judgement no punishment of the unbelievers will be removed? Ibn Kathir, it reports, observes that the phrase "could have one of two meanings." First, the conditional sense just given — *if* We grant your request and send you back, you will revert; which is exactly how 23:75 and 6:28 are framed. Second, that "removal of punishment" can describe a punishment whose causes are complete and whose arrival is imminent, then postponed for a few days — as with the people of Yūnus, peace be upon him, where the Qurʼān says "Surely We have removed from them their punishment" although the punishment had not yet arrived; only its signs were visible when it was delayed.

## Living it

**The trouble was never that the evidence was thin.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 9 is that "the certain truth has come to them, but they doubt it and do not believe in it" while playing about. Whatever else that describes, it is not a person short of information.

**Say "Allah knows best" when you do not know.** Ibn Masʿūd sat up from his rest at the sound of a confident speaker, and the first thing he reached for was 38:86 and the rule that admitting ignorance is itself part of knowledge — and that a man "should not pretend that he knows it." In a passage where the greatest scholars differ over the meaning of a single word and end with *Allah knows best*, that is not a side lesson; it is the method.

**Do not save your faith for the emergency.** The cry of ayah 12 is addressed to the right Lord in the right words, and it comes only when the punishment is already being witnessed. The answer the Qurʼān gives it, by Ibn Kathir's reading, is 6:27, 14:44, 89:23 and 34:51–52 — the remembrance that arrives too late to avail. Our task is to say *innā muʾminūn* now, while the sky is clear.

passages.title: Why the plea is refused, and the greatest blow
passages.tafsir:
**These four ayat are the answer to a desperate prayer — and the answer is no.**

In the ayah just before, people who witness the punishment cry out: *"Our Lord! Remove the torment from us, really we shall become believers!"* (ayah 12). Ibn Kathir explains that ayah simply: when the disbelievers witness the punishment of Allah, they will ask for it to be taken away from them. Ayat 13–16 are the reply. Allah does not argue with their words; He exposes them. The reminder already reached them (13). They answered it with insult (14). Lift the pressure and they will go straight back to what they were (15). What is left is the blow (16). That single movement — a plea, and four reasons why it changes nothing — is what holds these ayat together.

## Ayah 13: "How can they be reminded?"

*"How can there be for them an admonition, when a Messenger explaining things clearly has already come to them."*

Ibn Kathir gives the sense plainly: *"what further admonition do they need when We have sent them a Messenger with a clear Message and warning?"* The refusal is not "repentance is impossible for you." It is: the reminder you are now asking for was already delivered, and you know it.

Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat beside this one, both of which put the same question — *how?* — to people reaching for faith at the wrong moment: *"On that Day will man remember, but how will that remembrance (then) avail him?"* (89:23), and *"And if you could but see, when they will be terrified with no escape, and they will be seized from a near place. And they will say (in the Hereafter): 'We do believe (now);' but how could they receive (faith and its acceptance by Allah) from a place so far off..."* (34:51–52). He also places this passage alongside two ayat in which the same bargain is offered too late: *"Would that we were but sent back (to the world)! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers!"* (6:27), and the wrongdoers pleading, *"Our Lord! Respite us for a little while, we will answer Your Call and follow the Messengers!"* — answered with, *"Had you not sworn aforetime that you would not leave (the world for the Hereafter)"* (14:44).

Read together, these are not four separate scenes. They are one recurring scene: the request for more time, made by people who already had it.

**"A Messenger explaining things clearly."** The same word, *mubīn*, describes the smoke in ayah 10, which Ibn Kathir glosses as *"clearly visible, such that all people will see it."* Ibn Kathir's paraphrase of ayah 13 turns on exactly this: what more do they need, when the Message and the warning came to them clearly? Nothing was hidden; nothing was cryptic. That clarity is precisely what leaves them without excuse.

## Ayah 14: "One taught — a madman!"

*"Then they had turned away from him and said: '(He is) one taught, a madman!'"*

Ibn Kathir: *"Yet despite that, they turned away from him, opposed him and rejected him, and they said: (He is) one taught (by a human being), a madman."*

Notice the sequence the ayah insists on with *"then"*: first the Messenger came to them, **then** the turning away. This was not a first reaction to something strange; it came after clarity — which is what makes it turning *away* rather than never having looked.

And notice what they actually said. Ibn Kathir fills in the first charge: *"one taught"* means taught **by a human being** — that some person was the source. The second charge, *"a madman,"* says the opposite about the same man. Set side by side in a single breath, the two accusations pull against each other; a man coached by an informant is not a man out of his senses. This is what rejection sounds like when it is looking for a reason rather than following one. And these are the same people who, once the torment comes, will say "we shall become believers." Ayah 14 is the evidence that the promise in ayah 12 is not worth what it costs to say.

## Ayah 15: The reprieve that proved the point

*"Verily, We shall remove the torment for a while. Verily, you will revert."*

To feel this ayah you need the episode the Companions attached to it. It is the report of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him), narrated by Masruq: a man in the mosque of Kufah, at the gates of Kindah, was telling people what the "visible smoke" of ayah 10 would be — that it would come on the Day of Resurrection, taking away the hearing and sight of the hypocrites, while for the believers it would be like having a cold. Ibn Masʿud, who had been lying down, sat up with a start. He first quoted *"Say: 'No wage do I ask of you for this, nor am I one of the pretenders'"* (38:86), and drew from it a rule of knowledge: **when a man does not know something, he should say, "Allah knows best."** Then he gave his own account.

When the Quraysh did not respond to Islam and grew stubborn, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked Allah against them, that they would have years like the years of drought and famine of Yusuf. They became so exhausted and hungry that they ate bones and dead meat. When they looked at the sky, they saw nothing but smoke — in another report, "a man would look at the sky and he would see nothing between him and the sky except a smoky haze, because of his exhaustion." Then a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah! Pray to Allah to send rain to Mudar, for they are dying." So the Prophet ﷺ prayed for rain for them, and they got rain. And this ayah was revealed: *We shall remove the torment for a while — you will revert.* Ibn Masʿud then asked: *"Do you think that the torment will be removed for them on the Day of Resurrection? When they were granted ease, they reverted to their former state."* He also listed five things that had already come to pass: the smoke, the defeat of the Romans, the splitting of the moon, the *Batshah*, and the torment (*lizām*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties to *"the punishment will be inseparable from you,"* 25:77). This report was narrated in the Two Sahihs; it was also recorded by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, by At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i in their Books of Tafsir, and by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim with a number of chains of narration.

Sit with what happened there. Their request *was* answered. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for rain for the very people who had refused his call, and the rain came — and the relief changed nothing. That is the ayah's argument, in Ibn Masʿud's own summary: when they were granted ease, they reverted.

**Two ways the scholars read the ayah.** Ibn Kathir's first reading: *"if We were to remove the torment from you for a while, and send you back to the world, you would go back to your former state of disbelief and denial"* — the same verdict as *"And though We had mercy on them and removed the distress which is on them, still they would obstinately persist in their transgression, wandering blindly"* (23:75) and *"But if they were returned (to the world), they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars"* (6:28). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a second possible meaning from him: that all the causes of the punishment are already complete and the punishment is imminent, but it is postponed for a few days — as it was delayed in the case of the people of Yunus (peace be upon him), where only the signs of punishment were visible, and the Qur'an still describes that as a removal of punishment.

**Why this matters for the passage.** The Companions and their pupils differed over the "smoke" of ayah 10, and ayah 15 sits at the heart of that difference. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records three views. First: the smoke is a portent of the Day of Judgment, still to come — the view of al-Murtada, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Hurairah, Zaid ibn ʿAli, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Abi Mulaikah and others. Second: the prophecy has already occurred, in the Makkan drought and famine — the view of Ibn Masʿud and others, with whom a number of the Salaf concurred: Mujahid, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Ibrahim an-Nakhaʿi, ad-Dahhak and ʿAtiyah al-ʿAwfi, and this was also the view of Ibn Jarir. Third, from ʿAbdur-Rahman al-Aʿraj and others: the "smoke" was the dust stirred up over Makkah on the day of the Conquest — of which Ibn Kathir said, *"This view is gharib (unfamiliar), in fact munkar (against authentic reports)."*

The first two views are the popular ones, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that both are confirmed by authentic traditions. Ibn Kathir leans to the first, arguing that the plain wording *"covering mankind"* is too large for something the Makkans alone experienced: *"if it was only an illusion which happened to the idolators of Makkah, Allah would not have said 'covering mankind.'"* He supports it from the Sunnah — the report of Hudhayfah bin Asid al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said the Hour will not come until ten signs are seen, among them "the smoke," which was recorded only by Muslim in his Sahih; the incident recorded in the Two Sahihs in which the Prophet ﷺ said to Ibn Sayyad, *"I am concealing something for you,"* and Ibn Sayyad answered, "It is *Ad-Dukh*," and was told, *"Be off with you! You cannot get further than your rank"* — the concealed words being ayah 10; and a report from Abu Malik al-Ashʿari (may Allah be pleased with him) recorded by Ibn Jarir, of which Ibn Kathir said, "This chain of transmitters is good," warning of three things, the first a smoke that will cause only a cold in a believer but will permeate the entire body of an unbeliever.

The honest position is the one Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches: the first two views both rest on evidence, each objection has an answer, and — as it says — *"Allah knows best!"* And the practical force of ayah 15 survives either way, because on both readings the ayah says the same thing about the human heart. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the purpose of the reprieve directly: Allah, despite their false promise, will remove the punishment for a short while *in order to establish an argument against them, showing that they will not keep to their promise.* A reprieve given to someone who has already chosen is not a second chance. It is an exhibit.

## Ayah 16: The greatest blow

*"On the Day when We shall strike you with the great Batshah. Verily, We will exact retribution."*

The translations reach for the same idea in different words: *strike you with the great Batshah*, *the day We will seize (you) with the greatest seizure*, *the Day We will deal the fiercest blow.* And it is *al-kubrā*, "the great," "the greatest" — a word of comparison that quietly puts everything before it in its place. The famine was real; whatever they suffered was real. But it was not the greatest.

**What is this Day?** Ibn Masʿud interpreted it to mean the day of Badr, and the group who agreed with him about the smoke agreed here too; it was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas in a report related from al-ʿAwfi, and from Ubayy bin Kaʿb (may Allah be pleased with them). Ibn Kathir judges this *possible* — *"although the day of Badr was also a day of vengeance"* — but holds that *"the apparent meaning is that it refers to the Day of Resurrection."*

He then relays a report from Ibn Jarir, who said: *"Yaʿqub narrated to me; Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to me, Khalid al-Hadhdhaʼ narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, who said, 'Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him) said that 'the great Batshah' is the day of Badr, and I say that it is the Day of Resurrection."'"* Of this the tafsir text says only: *"This chain of narration is Sahih to him"* — it does not name who passed that judgement, so neither will we. This — the Day of Resurrection — was also the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, and of ʿIkrimah according to the more authentic of the two reports narrated from him. The passage closes, as we should close, with *"And Allah knows best."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the two readings together rather than pitting them against each other: Badr genuinely was a great seizure, "but that does not necessarily mean that a greater seizure will not be made on the Day of Judgment." It adds a principle worth keeping: whenever a punishment befell the enemies of the truth, the noble Companions took these ayat to apply to that particular punishment — and that does not negate the ayah's also pointing to the signs of the Hour. A warning in the Qur'an is not used up by its first instalment.

**"Verily, We will exact retribution."** The passage ends with Allah speaking of Himself. The renderings are *"We will exact retribution"* and *"We will take vengeance"* — and Ibn Kathir's remark that the day of Badr "was also a day of vengeance" shows how the word lands in history as well as at the end of time. This is not an outburst. It comes at the end of a sequence: a Messenger sent with a clear message, a warning delivered, a cry for relief answered with rain, and then the record of what they did with the relief.

## Living it

**Do not mistake a hard season for a changed heart.** These ayat are unsparing about faith that appears under pressure and disappears with it. Ibn Masʿud's summary is the whole lesson in nine words: *when they were granted ease, they reverted to their former state.* If your prayers deepen in illness, debt or fear, that is a mercy — but the test of what it was comes on the day the trouble lifts. Ask yourself honestly what you did with the last reprieve you were given.

**The reminder has already come.** Ayah 13 refuses the plea on the ground that a Messenger explaining things clearly had already come to them. For anyone who has heard the Qur'an and understood it, the door is open now, while walking through it still costs something. The parallel ayat Ibn Kathir gathers — 89:23, 34:51–52, 6:27, 14:44 — all describe the same thing: faith offered at the point where there is nothing left to choose.

**Watch how you dismiss what you would rather not accept.** The two accusations in ayah 14 do not fit together, and the men who made them said both anyway. When you find yourself reaching for any reason at all to put down a truth that makes demands of you, that is the moment ayah 14 is describing.

**And learn Ibn Masʿud's rule.** He sat up in alarm over a man speaking about this very passage without knowledge, and the first thing he taught was that saying "Allah knows best" is itself part of knowledge. The scholars here differed — over the smoke, over the Day of the great blow — and they differed with evidence, with attribution, and without pretending. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends its discussion the same way: *Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.* That restraint is part of what this passage teaches.

passages.title: Moses' summons to Pharaoh's people
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat lift us out of Makkah and set us down in Egypt. A proud people who had been given every worldly advantage were sent a messenger; this passage is his opening address to them, quoted almost entirely in his own voice. What holds ayat 17–21 together is that they are a single embassy: one messenger (ayah 17), one demand (ayah 18), one warning about the attitude that will decide their fate (ayah 19), and then — when the demand is met with menace — a prophet's twofold response: refuge with Allah, and a request simply to be left alone (ayat 20–21).

## "Before them"

Ayah 17 opens with a comparison rather than a story: *before them* We tested Pharaoh's people. Ibn Kathīr spells out both ends of it — Allah tells us, "before these idolators, We tested the people of Fir'awn, the copts of Egypt." The "them" is the idolators of the Prophet's ﷺ own city, whom the preceding ayat have been addressing.

That link is what makes the passage bite. Egypt is not a change of subject. It is the same case, tried once before, with the verdict already published: a people given a messenger and given proof, and still refusing.

## "A noble messenger" (ayah 17)

Ibn Kathīr identifies him at once: "means, Mūsā, peace be upon him, the one to whom Allah spoke."

Pause on that description. Of all the ways to introduce Mūsā, Ibn Kathīr reaches for the one thing that sets him apart — Allah addressed him with speech. The man standing before Pharaoh's court is not a man with a theory. He is a man who has been spoken to.

And the ayah calls him *karīm* — noble, honourable. The nobility is stated before the demand is made, and it matters: everything he is about to say is the speech of an honourable man, not an agitator.

## The demand, and the credential (ayah 18)

"Deliver to me the servants of Allah." Ibn Kathīr reads this exactly as the parallel address in Sūrah Ṭā Hā: *So let the Children of Israel go with us, and torment them not; indeed, we have come with a sign from your Lord! And peace will be upon him who follows the guidance* (20:47).

Notice how the enslaved people are named. Not "my people," not "the Hebrews," not "your labourers" — **the servants of Allah**. In one phrase the entire basis of Pharaoh's claim over them is dissolved. They are not his to keep; they belong to Another, and their Owner is asking for them back. Later in this same sūrah, Ibn Kathīr describes what Allah rescued them from: "their humiliation and subjugation at the hands of Fir'awn, when they were forced to do menial tasks." This was no abstract dispute over jurisdiction but the freeing of a broken people.

Then the credential: "Verily, I am to you a Messenger worthy of all trust" (*rasūl amīn*). Ibn Kathīr glosses it precisely — it means, "what I convey to you is trustworthy." The claim is not primarily about Mūsā's character in general; it is about the message in transit. Nothing has been added on the way, nothing withheld. A messenger's whole worth lies in his refusal to touch what he was given to carry.

## "And exalt not yourselves against Allah" (ayah 19)

This is the hinge of the passage. The obstacle Mūsā names is not ignorance, and not even their attachment to their own gods — it is self-exaltation. Ibn Kathīr: "and do not be too arrogant to follow His signs. Accept His proof and believe in His evidence."

He connects it to Allah's words in Sūrah Ghāfir: *Verily, those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation* (40:60). The pattern is exact and worth sitting with — the one who is too high to bow is brought in low. Arrogance is not merely punished; it is reversed.

And the warning turns out to be the diagnosis. Later in this same sūrah, Allah's own verdict on Pharaoh is delivered in that very word: he *was arrogant* — literally, exalting himself. Ibn Kathīr explains, "he was proud and stubborn," citing *Verily, Fir'awn exalted himself in the land* (28:4) and *but they behaved insolently and they were people self-exalting* (23:46), and adds that "he was one of the excessive and held a foolish opinion of himself." Mūsā told them in ayah 19 precisely which disease would kill them, and they died of it.

"Truly, I have come to you with a manifest authority" — *sulṭān mubīn*. Ibn Kathīr: "with clear and obvious proof. This refers to the clear signs and definitive evidence with which Allah sent him." Note what this rules out. Mūsā is not asking for blind loyalty, and he does not offer submission as an alternative to evidence. He brings the proof, and then asks that pride not be allowed to overrule it. Unbelief here is not an intellectual failure; it is the refusal to be seen accepting something from someone else's hand.

## "I seek refuge with my Lord and your Lord" (ayah 20)

The court's answer to all this can be read off Mūsā's next sentence: they threatened him. He responds not by threatening back, but by taking shelter.

The scholars differ over what exactly he feared, because the Arabic word *rajm* carries more than one sense. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Ṣāliḥ said it "refers to a verbal assault, which means insults." Qatādah took it in the literal sense of stoning, and expressed the ayah's force beautifully: "I seek refuge with Allah, Who created me and you, from your making any harmful words or actions reach me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *rajm* means "to stone to death," and also "to revile or to make a verbal assault or to heap up insults"; both senses are possible here, but the literal one seems more likely, "because Fir'aun's people must have been threatening Prophet Musa with death."

Two things in this ayah deserve to be felt rather than merely understood.

First, **"my Lord and your Lord."** Under threat of death, Mūsā still will not let go of the one truth he came with. Even his cry for protection is a lesson to them: the One I am hiding behind is the One who made you too. Qatādah's wording captures it — *Who created me and you*.

Second, **a prophet holding manifest proof still seeks refuge.** Certainty does not make a servant self-sufficient. The strongest thing Mūsā can do in that room is not to argue harder; it is to place himself behind Allah. That is *istiʿādha*, seeking refuge — and here it appears as the natural reflex of a man who has done everything he was asked to do and is now being threatened for it.

## "Then keep away from me and leave me alone" (ayah 21)

The last ayah of the passage is startling in its restraint. Ibn Kathīr paraphrases: "then let us leave one another alone and live in peace until Allah judges between us."

Mūsā does not withdraw the message; he has already delivered it, and the proof stands. What he asks them to withdraw is their hands. If you will not believe, at least stop attacking. It is a request for room to exist — and it quietly leaves the verdict where it belongs: *until Allah judges between us*.

Ibn Kathīr then tells us what came of that request, and it is the most sobering detail in the passage: "After Mūsā, peace be upon him, had stayed among them for a long time, and the proof of Allah had been established against them, and that only increased them in disbelief and stubbornness, he prayed to his Lord against them, a prayer which was answered."

**A long time.** The invocation Ibn Kathīr cites from Sūrah Yūnus — *Our Lord! Destroy their wealth, and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful torment* — and Allah's reply, *Verily, the invocation of you both is accepted. So you both keep to the straight way* (10:88–89), came only after long patient calling, not at the first insult.

That is the moral order of this passage: proof first, patience long, prayer last.

## Living it

- **Carry the message intact.** *Rasūl amīn*, as Ibn Kathīr reads it, is about the trustworthiness of what is conveyed. Whoever passes on knowledge of the dīn inherits that standard: deliver it as you received it, without improving it to suit the room.
- **Watch for self-exaltation in yourself.** Ayah 19 warns against the arrogance that will not accept a proof because of whose hand is holding it. Pharaoh's people are the extreme case; the mechanism is ordinary and domestic — the argument you cannot concede because conceding costs face.
- **Answer threat with refuge.** Mūsā's response to intimidation was, "I seek refuge with my Lord and your Lord." Not paralysis, not retaliation — refuge, and then carrying on.
- **Ask for peace where belief is refused.** Ayah 21 permits stepping back from hostility without stepping back from the truth, and leaves the judgment to Allah, where it was always going to be settled.

passages.title: Pharaoh drowned, his luxuries left behind
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat carry the story of Musa and Fir'awn to its end: a prophet's exhausted prayer, a night escape, a sea deliberately left open, an empire drowned in a single morning, and an estate of gardens and fine dwellings handed to somebody else — with not one tear shed anywhere in creation. What holds them together is a single movement from **word** to **verdict**: ayah 22 is the last thing Musa says to his Lord about this people, and everything after it is Allah acting.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Ibn Kathir opens this section by explaining what Allah is doing with the story. Allah, he says, is telling us: "before these idolators, We tested the people of Fir'awn, the Copts of Egypt." So the account that follows is not offered as a piece of ancient history. It is placed *before* the people the sūrah is addressing, as a case already tried: a great civilisation, a great messenger sent to it, and what became of it.

The immediately preceding ayat (17–21) set the scene. A **noble Messenger** came to them — Ibn Kathir identifies him as Musa, peace be upon him, "the one to whom Allah spoke." His demand was simple: *"Deliver to me the servants of Allah"* — which Ibn Kathir reads exactly as the parallel elsewhere, *"So let the Children of Israel go with us, and torment them not"* (20:47). He told them he was a messenger **worthy of all trust** — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, "what I convey to you is trustworthy." He warned them not to **exalt themselves against Allah**, which Ibn Kathir explains as: do not be too arrogant to follow His signs; accept His proof and believe in His evidence — the same disease Allah names in *"Verily, those who scorn My worship they will surely enter Hell in humiliation"* (40:60). And he came with **manifest authority**: clear, obvious proof, the signs and definitive evidence Allah sent with him.

Then the threat. Musa says he seeks refuge with "my Lord and your Lord" lest they **stone** him (*tarjumūn*, from *rajm*). The scholars read that word two ways. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said it refers to a verbal assault — insults. Qatadah took it literally: "I seek refuge with Allah, Who created me and you, from your making any harmful words or actions reach me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *rajm* carries both senses — to stone to death, and to revile and heap up insults — but judges the literal sense more likely here, because Fir'awn's people must have been threatening Musa, peace be upon him, with death. Either way, notice where he goes with the fear: not to a bodyguard, but to *"my Lord **and your Lord**"* — even in terror he keeps preaching Allah's oneness to the very men threatening him.

His last offer, in ayah 21, is almost gentle: *if you do not believe me, then keep away from me and leave me alone* — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, "then let us leave one another alone and live in peace until Allah judges between us."

## Ayah 22 — the prayer of a man who has run out of road

Ibn Kathir gives the timing precisely, and it matters. Musa "had stayed among them for a long time, and the proof of Allah had been established against them, and that only increased them in disbelief and stubbornness." Only *then* "he prayed to his Lord against them, a prayer which was answered."

So *fa-daʿā rabbahu* — "then he called upon his Lord" — is not a flash of temper. It comes at the end of a long process: calling, signs, argument, an offer of peaceful separation, all met with hardening. The prayer against a people is the last door, not the first.

And look at the words the ayah records: *"These are indeed the people who are criminals"* (*qawmun mujrimūn*). Here Musa lays the case before his Lord and stops — no sentence is named in this ayah. Ibn Kathir does connect it with the fuller version of his supplication elsewhere: *"Our Lord! You have indeed bestowed on Fir'awn and his chiefs splendour and wealth in the life of this world... Our Lord! Destroy their wealth, and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful torment"* — and Allah's reply, *"Verily, the invocation of you both is accepted. So you both keep to the straight way"* (10:88–89).

Note the shape of that answer. The prayer is accepted — and in the same breath the two brothers are told to *keep to the straight way*. An answered prayer is not a discharge from obedience. It raises the standard.

## Ayah 23 — "Depart with My servants by night"

Allah's response to the prayer is a command to move. Ibn Kathir puts the point sharply: Allah "commanded him to bring the Children of Israel out from among them, **without the command, consent or permission of Fir'awn**."

Feel the language. These were people held, in Ibn Kathir's words on the ayat that follow, in "humiliation and subjugation at the hands of Fir'awn, when they were forced to do menial tasks." Allah calls them *ʿibādī* — **My servants**. The whole dispute is settled in a possessive pronoun. And the parallel ayah Ibn Kathir cites fills in what the night journey would involve: *"Travel by night with My servants and strike a dry path for them in the sea, fearing neither to be overtaken nor being afraid"* (20:77).

Then the strangest half of the command: *"Surely, you will be pursued."* Allah tells them in advance that the army is coming. He does not remove the pursuit; He removes the surprise. Obedience here means walking out into a night you have been told will have hooves behind it.

## Ayah 24 — the sea left open

This is the passage's most humanly recognisable moment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the key word: *rahwan* means "to be still, calm, motionless." Then it tells the scene, citing Ibn Kathir: when Musa, peace be upon him, and his companions had crossed the sea, he "naturally desired for the sea to go back to its original state. So he wanted to strike it with his staff so that it would form a barrier between them and Fir'aun to prevent him from reaching them."

That is the sane, obvious instinct — close the door behind you. And Allah tells him: *leave it*. Leave the sea as it is, quiet and divided. Ibn 'Abbas explained *"leave the sea as it is"* to mean: **leave it as it is and keep moving.** Mujahid said *rahwan* means "a dry path, as it is — do not command it to go back; leave it until the last of them have entered it." Ibn Kathir reports the same view from 'Ikrimah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Ka'b Al-Ahbar and Simak bin Harb.

The open road that looks like a fatal security lapse *is the trap*. The corridor Musa wanted to shut is what draws the army in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completes it: when Fir'awn and his host reach the middle of the dry path, Allah causes the water to flow, and they drown.

And Allah gives Musa the outcome as glad tidings before it happens: *"Verily, they are a host to be drowned"* — *jundun mughraqūn*. The drowning is spoken of as settled while the army is still riding. Ibn Kathir notes the double reassurance in it: he need fear neither being overtaken by Fir'awn nor drowning in the sea.

**What this asks of a believer:** sometimes obedience means leaving open the very thing you desperately want to close. Musa's instinct was reasonable, and Allah's command overrode it — because Musa was managing a threat while Allah was ending one.

## Ayat 25–27 — the inventory of what they left behind

Now the camera turns away from the water and pans, slowly, over an empty country. *Kam tarakū* — "**how many**" — is an exclamation, not a question. It invites you to stand in the abandoned estate and count.

- **Gardens, springs and green crops** (ayat 25–26) — Ibn Kathir treats these together and glosses the whole stretch by noting that it takes in the rivers and wells: the water that made that land rich in the first place.
- **Goodly places** (ayah 26) — *maqām karīm*, which Ibn Kathir renders as "fine dwellings and beautiful places." Mujahid and Sa'id bin Jubayr said it means **elevated places** — the high seats, the positions of honour, the addresses that announced who you were.
- **Comforts of life wherein they used to take delight** (ayah 27) — *naʿma kānū fīhā fākihīn*. Ibn Kathir unpacks it as "a life which they were enjoying, where they could eat whatever they wanted and wear what they liked, with wealth and glory and power in the land."

Then his verdict, which is the hinge of the whole passage: **"Then all of that was taken away in a single morning, they departed from this world and went to Hell, what a terrible abode!"**

That is the argument the sūrah is making to anyone reading it. Not that gardens and fine houses are evil, but that they are *leaveable* — and that the interval between owning the world and standing in the Fire can be one morning long. The verb *tarakū*, "they left behind," is the same verb Musa was given in ayah 24 for the sea. They left; it stayed.

## Ayah 28 — "And We made other people inherit them"

*Kadhālika* — "thus it was" — and then the estate changes hands. Who inherited it? Ibn Kathir: "namely the Children of Israel." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is stated explicitly in Sūrah ash-Shuʿarāʼ, and notes the objection some raise — that there is no historical evidence that the Children of Israel ever settled in Egypt again — recording that this objection has been rebutted in its commentary on Sūrah ash-Shuʿarāʼ.

The point stands regardless: the people who had been forced into menial tasks became the heirs. Ownership does not belong to whoever currently holds the deeds; it is passed from hand to hand by Allah.

## Ayah 29 — and nobody wept

This is the ayah that lingers. The tyrant's end is recorded — and then the Qur'an mentions, of all things, the *absence of mourning*. **"And the heavens and the earth wept not for them."**

Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism: "they had no righteous deeds which used to ascend through the gates of the heavens, which would weep for them when they died, and they had no places on earth where they used to worship Allah which would notice their loss."

The clearest exposition comes in a report Ibn Jarir recorded from Sa'id bin Jubayr. A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and asked about this very ayah — *do the heavens and the earth weep for anybody?* Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

> "Yes, there is no one who does not have a gate in the heavens through which his provision comes down and his good deeds ascend. When the believer dies, that gate is closed; it misses him and weeps for him, and the place of prayer on earth where he used to pray and remember Allah also weeps for him. But the people of Fir'awn left no trace of righteousness on the earth and they had no good deeds that ascended to Allah, so the heavens and the earth did not weep for them."

Al-'Awfi reported something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

### From the Sunnah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the reports behind this, noting that several ahadith confirm that when a righteous person dies, the heaven and earth weep. **Abu Yaʿla** reports on the authority of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: *"For every person there are two gates in the heaven. Through one of them his sustenance descends, and through the other his deeds and his conversation ascend. When he dies, the gates remember him and weep"* — and the Prophet ﷺ then recited this very ayah as evidence for what he had said. **Ibn Jarir** records that Shuraih ibn 'Ubaid al-Hadrami, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"If a believer dies away from home where there is no one to weep for him, the heaven and earth weep for him"* — again reciting ayah 29, and adding that neither the sky nor the earth weeps for a non-believer. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, also held that the heaven and the earth weep for a righteous person.

### Where the scholars differed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records both positions. **Some scholars** take the ayah **metaphorically**: the sky and earth do not really weep in the primary sense of the word; the point is that these people's existence was so insignificant that when they were wiped out it caused grief to no one. **Others** — and this is the view Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself prefers — take it in its **primary, real sense**, reasoning that where the literal meaning of an expression is possible there is no need to shift it to the figurative, and that the narrations above support the plain sense.

To the objection that the heavens and the earth have no faculty of sense with which to weep, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers from the Qur'an itself: *"And there is not a single thing that does not extol His purity and praise, but you do not understand their extolling"* (17:44) — every member of the universe has some sense, to a higher or lower degree.

And then it draws the line exactly where it should be drawn: it is not necessary that the heavens and earth weep *in the same way human beings do*. "The way of their weeping would surely be different from humans but we are unaware of its reality." That is the sound approach — affirm what the revelation affirms, refuse to force it into the shape of created things, and leave the how of it to Allah.

**"Nor were they given respite."** *Wa mā kānū munẓarīn* — no reprieve, no stay of execution. Ibn Kathir gives the reason: "they did not deserve to be given a respite, because of their disbelief, sin, transgression and stubbornness." Respite had already been given, and given, and given — through the whole long time Musa stood among them.

## Living with these ayat

**You have a gate.** According to the report from Ibn 'Abbas, there is no one who does not have a gate in the heavens — provision coming down, good deeds going up; and in the report Abu Yaʿla brings from Anas, two gates, one for sustenance descending and one for deeds and speech ascending. The question is not whether you have one, but whether anything is going *up* it. Fir'awn's people had gates too. Nothing ascended through them that was worth missing.

**You have a place.** The earth weeps for the spot where a servant used to pray and remember Allah. That is a startling thought about the prayer mat in the corner of your house, the row in the masjid you keep, the desk where you make dhikr. These are places that will notice you are gone. Fir'awn's people "left no trace of righteousness on the earth" — and the inventory in ayat 25–27 shows how much they had built.

**One morning.** Gardens, springs, green crops, elevated places, food they chose and clothes they liked, glory and power in the land — and Ibn Kathir's summary is that all of it was taken away in a single morning. Nothing in that list is forbidden to own. All of it is filed under the verb *tarakū*: **they left it behind.**

passages.title: Israel delivered, chosen, and tested
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close the story of Musa and Fir'awn by turning away from the drowned tyrant and onto the people he had crushed. Fir'awn's court has just vanished — its gardens, springs, crops and fine places left behind, its people unmourned by heaven and earth (ayat 25–29). Now Allah tells us what became of the enslaved: rescued (30), rescued *from a named man* (31), then chosen (32), and finally granted signs that were themselves a trial (33). What holds the passage together is a single movement: **from humiliation, to honour, to responsibility.**

## Where we are in the story

Ibn Kathir sets the scene for the whole section: Allah is telling the idolaters that "before these idolators, We tested the people of Fir'awn, the copts of Egypt." A "noble Messenger" came to them — Musa, peace be upon him, "the one to whom Allah spoke" — with one demand: *Deliver to me the servants of Allah* (ayah 18), which Ibn Kathir reads as Musa's words elsewhere: "So let the Children of Israel go with us, and torment them not" (20:47). The entire confrontation was about these people. Fir'awn would not release them; after Musa had stayed among them a long time and Allah's proof had been established — which only increased them in disbelief and stubbornness — he prayed to his Lord against them, "a prayer which was answered." Allah then commanded him to bring the Children of Israel out from among them, Ibn Kathir notes pointedly, "without the command, consent or permission of Fir'awn."

Then the sea. Ibn Kathir explains that once Musa and the Children of Israel had crossed, Musa wanted to strike the water with his staff so it would go back as it had been and form a barrier between them and Fir'awn. Allah commanded him instead to leave it *rahwan* — quiet and divided, exactly as it was — and gave him the glad tidings that Fir'awn's men were "a host to be drowned," and that he should fear neither being overtaken nor drowning. Ibn 'Abbas said the phrase means "leave it as it is and keep moving"; Mujahid explained it as a dry path left undisturbed: "Do not command it to go back; leave it until the last of them have entered it" — a reading also held by 'Ikrimah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Ka'b Al-Ahbar and Simak bin Harb. The open sea was not a gap left in the defences. Musa was told not to shield himself, because Allah had already told him how this ended.

Ayah 30 is the verdict on that night.

## Ayah 30 — "We certainly delivered"

Notice who the actor is. The verb is *najjaynā* — **We** delivered. Musa led them out; Allah saved them. Nothing in the escape is credited to Israelite courage, planning or numbers.

What they were saved from is *al-'adhāb al-muhīn*, the **humiliating** torment. Ibn Kathir explains: "Here Allah reminds them of how He saved them from their humiliation and subjugation at the hands of Fir'awn, when they were forced to do menial tasks." Humiliation and subjugation, and menial labour forced on them — this was suffering that fell on the dignity of a people as much as on their bodies.

Set that against the passing of their oppressors two ayat earlier. Ibn Kathir, on the gardens, springs, crops, "fine dwellings and beautiful places" (Mujahid and Sa'id bin Jubayr: "elevated places") and the comforts they delighted in — "a life which they were enjoying, where they could eat whatever they wanted and wear what they liked, with wealth and glory and power in the land" — writes: "Then all of that was taken away in a single morning, they departed from this world and went to Hell, what a terrible abode!"

And nothing in creation mourned them. Ibn Kathir explains that they had no righteous deeds ascending through the gates of heaven that would weep for them when they died, and no places on earth where they used to worship Allah that would notice their loss — "so they did not deserve to be given a respite, because of their disbelief, sin, transgression and stubbornness." Ibn Jarir recorded from Sa'id bin Jubayr that a man asked Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) whether the heavens and the earth really weep for anybody. He answered: yes — there is no one who does not have a gate in the heavens through which his provision comes down and his good deeds ascend; when the believer dies that gate is closed, it misses him and weeps for him, and the place of prayer on earth where he used to pray and remember Allah weeps for him too. But the people of Fir'awn "left no trace of righteousness on the earth."

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds that Hafiz Abu Ya'la reports on the authority of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: "For every person there are two gates in the heaven/sky. Through one of them his sustenance descends, and through the other his deeds and his conversation ascend. When he dies, the gates remember him and weep" — and that the Prophet ﷺ then recited this very verse as evidence. Ma'ārif notes that some scholars read the weeping figuratively, taking the verse to mean that these people were so insignificant that their being wiped out grieved no one; but in the light of these narrations it prefers the real, primary sense, on the principle that if the literal meaning of an expression is possible there is no need to interpret it metaphorically. It adds, importantly, that the heavens and the earth need not weep in the way human beings do: "The way of their weeping would surely be different from humans but we are unaware of its reality."

That is the contrast ayah 30 lands in. Heaven and earth did not weep for the tyrants; the humiliated were personally delivered by their Lord.

## Ayah 31 — the torment had a name

Ayah 31 does something worth pausing over: it ties the torment to a person. *Min fir'awn* — "of Pharaoh." The oppression is not left as an abstract misfortune or an unlucky age; it is traced to one man, and then his character is stated plainly.

**"He was truly a tyrant" — *kāna 'āliyan*.** Ibn Kathir renders it: "he was proud and stubborn," and links it to "Verily, Fir'awn exalted himself in the land" (28:4) and to "but they behaved insolently and they were people self-exalting" (23:46). Not simply confidence — a man who has placed himself above correction.

**"A transgressor" — *min al-musrifīn*.** Ibn Kathir sums him up in a single line: "He was one of the excessive and held a foolish opinion of himself." The two descriptions sit together naturally: pride is what such a man carries inside, excess is what it produces outside.

Earlier in the same sūrah, Musa's message to these very people had included the warning *And exalt not yourselves against Allah* (19). Ibn Kathir glosses that as: "do not be too arrogant to follow His signs. Accept His proof and believe in His evidence," citing "Verily, those who scorn My worship they will surely enter Hell in humiliation!" (40:60). Fir'awn had been told, in plain words, what would ruin him.

## Ayah 32 — chosen, and chosen "with knowledge"

*"And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others."* Two phrases carry the weight.

**"Above the worlds" (*'alā al-'ālamīn*).** Taken flatly this could sound like an unconditional supremacy. The early commentators read it as superiority over their contemporaries. Mujahid said it means "they were chosen above those among whom they lived." Qatadah said, "They were chosen above the other people of their own time," adding that "in every period there are people who are chosen above others." Ibn Kathir supports this with two parallels using the same idiom: Allah said to Musa, "O Musa I have chosen you above men" (7:144) — meaning above the people of his time; and to Maryam, "and Allah has chosen you above the women of the nations" (3:42) — meaning she was chosen above the women of her time. Ibn Kathir observes that Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her) is higher than her in status or equal to her, as was Asiyah bint Muzahim, the wife of Fir'awn; and that the superiority of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) over all other women is like the superiority of *tharīd* over all other dishes.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān states the conclusion directly: this verse "does not imply that the Children of Israel are superior to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ," because it means they were given superiority over all the people of their time — exactly as with Maryam. It allows that they may have some sort of superiority across all ages "from a particular angle," but that "collectively the Ummah of the Final Messenger ﷺ holds the highest status."

Qatadah's addition is worth sitting with: in every period there are people chosen above others. Being chosen belongs to a time and a task.
