**"With knowledge" (*'alā 'ilm*).** This is the phrase that keeps the whole thing from looking arbitrary. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān explains it as meaning that "every work of Allah has wisdom. Thus wisdom underlying Allah's knowledge dictated that they be granted superiority, and they were granted accordingly." The choice was not blind or sentimental. It issued from His knowledge and His wisdom.

## Ayah 33 — the gift that was also a test

*"And We showed them signs in which there was a clear test."*

**The signs.** Ibn Kathir: *āyāt* here means "clear proofs and extraordinary evidence." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān, citing Qurtubi, specifies that "the word 'signs' refers to the miracles of the staff, the shining hand and others." These were not subtle hints — a staff, a shining hand, and a sea left standing open while an army drowned in it.

**The word *balā'*.** Here is where the ayah turns. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān, again citing Qurtubi, notes that *balā'* has two senses — **blessing** and **trial** — and that "here both senses are possible." That is not scholarly hesitation; it is the point. Ibn Kathir takes the trial sense and makes it concrete: a plain trial means "an obvious test to show who would be guided by it."

So the sequence of the passage completes itself. They were delivered (30) from a named oppressor (31), chosen by a decision made with knowledge and wisdom (32), and then granted clear proofs — which were at once the greatest favour and the sharpest examination (33). A sign leaves no one where it found them.

## Living it

**Deliverance is not achievement.** Read ayah 30 as your own biography. Whatever you were pulled out of — a humiliation, a fear, a situation you could not have escaped by your own strength — the verb is *najjaynā*, "We delivered." Gratitude is the only honest response; self-congratulation is a misreading of the text.

**Watch the two words used for Fir'awn.** "Proud and stubborn," and "one of the excessive," who "held a foolish opinion of himself" — Ibn Kathir's phrases describe a disease with mild early forms available to anyone with a little power over another person: an employee, a child, someone who cannot answer back. And the sūrah's warning *do not exalt yourselves against Allah*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as refusing out of pride to follow His signs and accept His proof, is a temptation for the learned and the comfortable, not only for kings.

**Honour is tied to a time and a task.** On Qatadah's reading, in every period there are people chosen above others — and Ma'ārif is explicit that the highest collective standing belongs to the Ummah of the Final Messenger ﷺ. What is asked of anyone given standing is that the signs be received as signs.

**Every blessing is a *balā'*.** If *balā'* carries both blessing and trial, then the safety, health, wealth or knowledge you have been given is not the end of your examination but the form it currently takes. The question ayah 33 puts to its first audience — who will be guided by what they have been shown? — is still open, and it is put to us with a Book in our hands.

passages.title: Nothing beyond our first death
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat put the idolaters of Makkah on record. Ayah 34 announces that they *say* something; ayat 35–36 quote it in their own words — there is nothing beyond this first death, and if you claim otherwise, produce our dead fathers here and now; and ayah 37 answers not with an argument but with a name out of their own history: **the people of Tubbaʿ**. The unit holds together as a single movement: a denial, a challenge, and a warning drawn from a ruin the Arabs already knew about.

## Ayah 34: their words, entered into the record

**إِنَّ هَٰؤُلَاءِ لَيَقُولُونَ** — *"Indeed, these ˹Meccans˺ say…"*

The ayah does not yet tell us what they said. It tells us that they said it, and that Allah is about to repeat it back to them. Ibn Kathir places this whole passage under a single heading — **the refutation of those who deny the Resurrection** — and explains that here Allah denounces the idolaters for that denial and for their belief that there is nothing after this life, no life and no resurrection after death.

Notice what is *not* happening. Their position is not being summarised for them, softened, or restated in someone else's words. It is quoted. A claim that will not survive being said out loud in the presence of the truth is being given the chance to say itself out loud. The next two ayat are their own sentence, and ayah 37 is the reply.

## Ayah 35: the denial

**إِنْ هِيَ إِلَّا مَوْتَتُنَا الْأُولَىٰ وَمَا نَحْنُ بِمُنشَرِينَ**
*"There is nothing beyond our first death, and we shall not be resurrected."*

This is the belief Ibn Kathir named: nothing after this life — no life, and no resurrection after death. Death, on this view, is not a door but a wall.

## Ayah 36: the challenge — and why it proves nothing

What made them so sure? Ibn Kathir identifies the evidence they leaned on: **their forefathers had died and had not returned.** From that they built their demand:

> فَأْتُوا بِآبَائِنَا إِن كُنتُمْ صَادِقِينَ
> *"Then bring back our forefathers, if you speak the truth!"*

It sounds like a devastating test. It is not. Ibn Kathir calls it **"false evidence and a specious argument"** — that is, an argument that looks convincing on the surface and collapses the moment it is examined.

Why it collapses: the Resurrection was never claimed to happen *in this world*. It happens **on the Day of Judgement**, says Ibn Kathir, when this world has ended and ceased to be. Then Allah will bring all creatures back, created anew. So demanding a resurrection today, inside a world that is still running, is demanding something that was never promised, and then treating its absence as a refutation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking observation about the silence that follows: **Allah did not give an answer to this argument of theirs at all** — because it was too obvious to need explanation. The Qurʼān quotes the objection and moves straight on to ayah 37. Sometimes the strongest reply to a bad argument is to let it stand in the open where everyone can see it.

Maʿārif then sharpens the flaw in logical terms, quoting *Bayān-ul-Qurʼān*:

> **the negation of a particular thing does not necessarily imply the negation of a general thing.**

Unpack that. Life and death *in this world* are bound by specific natural laws and by wisdom, as Maʿārif puts it. That Allah is not, at this moment, bringing back to life those who died long ago says nothing whatever about whether He is able to give life after death in the Hereafter. The idolaters observed one particular case — dead men do not walk back into Makkah — and leapt to a universal denial. That leap is the whole of their reasoning, and it does not hold.

There is something worth carrying away here for anyone who meets a modern version of the same objection. "Show me a resurrection now, or I will not believe in one later" mistakes a specific arrangement of this world for a limit on the power of the One who arranged it.

Ibn Kathir also gestures at what that Day will hold: Allah will make the evildoers fuel for the fire of Hell, and on that Day, in the words of his commentary, "you will be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger will be a witness over you." The very ones demanding proof will one day stand inside the proof.

## Ayah 37: a question that is really a warning

**أَهُمْ خَيْرٌ أَمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ وَالَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ** — *"Are they better, or the people of Tubbaʿ, and those before them?"*

Ibn Kathir reads this as a threat and a warning: Allah is reminding them of the irresistible torment suffered by other idolaters who, like them, denied the Resurrection. The people of Tubbaʿ — that is, **Sabaʼ** — were destroyed, their land wrecked, and they themselves scattered here and there throughout the land, as Ibn Kathir notes was already covered in Sūrat Sabaʼ. He states the cause directly: **this was brought about because the idolaters denied the Resurrection.** And then the parallel: "Here too, the idolaters are compared to them."

The comparison lands close to home. Ibn Kathir points out the shared blood: the people of Tubbaʿ were **Arabs descended from Qaḥṭān**, just as Quraysh were **Arabs descended from ʿAdnān**. This is not some distant foreign nation being invoked. These were fellow Arabs. The ayah closes with the reason for their ruin: *"We destroyed them because they were indeed criminals."*

## Who was Tubbaʿ?

Here the sources open up, and it is worth following, because "Tubbaʿ" is easily misread as a personal name.

**It is a title, not a man.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: Tubbaʿ is not the name of a particular individual, but is said to be the royal title of the kings of Ḥimyar in Yemen. Ibn Kathir explains the custom: among the people of Ḥimyar — also known as Sabaʼ — when a man became their king, they called him Tubbaʿ, just as the title Chosroes was given to the king of Persia, Caesar to the king of the Romans, Firʿawn to the disbelieving ruler of Egypt, and Negus to the king of Ethiopia. Maʿārif adds that the plural is *Tabābiʿah*, so one speaks of the Tabābiʿah of Yemen; they held sway over Ḥimyar, Arabia, Syria, ʿIrāq and parts of Africa for a long time, with the western part of Yemen as their capital.

Because it is a title, Maʿārif notes that it is not clear which of the Tabābiʿah is meant here. It judges **Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Kathir's research and conclusion the most plausible**: that the reference is to **Tubbaʿ Awsaṭ (the Middle Tubbaʿ), whose name was Asʿad Abū Kurayb ibn Maʿdīkarib al-Yamānī**, a king who ruled at least seven hundred years before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and who reigned longest among the Ḥimyarī kings.

Maʿārif also observes that the people of Tubbaʿ are mentioned only twice in the Qurʼān — here and in Sūrah Qāf — and in both places only the name appears, with no chronicle attached. That silence is precisely why the commentators went looking.

## The king who came to Madinah

Ibn Kathir tells the story, and Maʿārif tells it again citing the narration of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq. This Tubbaʿ left Yemen on a journey of conquest, expanding his kingdom and domain until he reached **Samarqand**; he is the one who founded **al-Ḥīrah**.

It is agreed that he passed through **al-Madīnah** in the days of Jāhiliyyah, and he meant to take it. What happened next is one of the strangest details in this history: he fought its inhabitants and they resisted him — **they fought him by day and supplied him with food by night.** They would not surrender, and they would not let him go hungry. Ibn Kathir says he felt ashamed before them and refrained from harming them.

With him were **two Jewish rabbis** who advised him. They told him he would never prevail over this city — **because it was the place to which a Prophet would migrate towards the end of time.** He withdrew and took the two rabbis with him back to Yemen.

Passing by **Makkah**, he formed a second intention: to destroy the Kaʿbah. The rabbis told him not to do that either. They explained the significance of this House — that it had been built by **Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl**, peace be upon him — and that it would become of great importance through that same Prophet who would be sent towards the end of time. So the king honoured it instead: **he performed ṭawāf around it and covered it with a fine cloth.**

Then he returned to Yemen and invited its people to follow the religion of guidance along with him, and they accepted it. Ibn Kathir is careful about what that religion was at that point in history: this was before the coming of the Messiah, peace be upon him, and **the religion of Mūsā, peace be upon him, was the religion followed by those who were guided.** Maʿārif adds that it was the two rabbis who invited him to the Mosaic religion and that he accepted, and his people were influenced by him and accepted it too.

Maʿārif completes the arc: after his death his people went astray, reverting to idolatry and fire-worship, and **that** brought down the divine wrath whose details are given in Sūrah Sabaʼ.

Pause on the shape of it. A pagan king, seven centuries early, turned away from a city and a sanctuary by news of a Prophet not yet born — and he accepted the news, while his own people afterwards, and the Quraysh living beside that same Kaʿbah, did not.

## Why the ayah says "the people of Tubbaʿ"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a precise wording: on **both** occasions the Qurʼān refers to *the people of* Tubbaʿ — **قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ** — and not to Tubbaʿ himself. The commentary reads this as significant: the incident shows that this Tubbaʿ had himself embraced Islam, and it was his people who later went astray.

That reading is supported, Maʿārif says, by the narratives of **Sayyidnā Sahl ibn Saʿd** and **Ibn ʿAbbās**, may Allah be pleased with them, recorded by **Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Imām Aḥmad, Ṭabarānī and others**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"Do not revile Tubbaʿ, because he had embraced Islam."**

Ibn Kathir carries the same restraint from two further reports. **ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded** that Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"I do not know whether Tubbaʿ was a Prophet or not."** And it was narrated that Tamīm ibn ʿAbdur-Raḥmān said that **ʿAṭāʼ ibn Abī Rabāḥ** said: *"Do not revile Tubbaʿ, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade reviling him."* Ibn Kathir closes the discussion with the scholar's formula: **and Allah knows best.**

There is a lesson in that phrase sitting at the end of a long historical excursus. Where revelation stopped short, the Prophet ﷺ himself declined to fill in the blank — and the community was forbidden from speaking ill of a man whose standing with Allah they did not know.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of us.

**Test your objections the way Ibn Kathir tested theirs.** An argument can feel airtight and still be, in his words, *false evidence and a specious argument*. "I have never seen it happen, therefore it cannot happen" is the exact structure the Qurʼān quotes here and then leaves standing without a reply, because its weakness is self-evident.

**Do not confuse the rules of this world with the limits of Allah's power.** Maʿārif's principle is portable: life and death here run by specific laws and wisdom, and what does not occur under that arrangement tells you nothing about what Allah will do in the Hereafter.

**Take the warning of ayah 37 personally.** Quraysh were asked whether they were *better* than a people who were destroyed — fellow Arabs, whose kings' reach had extended as far as Samarqand — and destroyed, Ibn Kathir says, over this very denial. Ayah 37 gives the reason plainly: *"We destroyed them because they were indeed criminals."* Not lineage, not empire, not standing beside the Kaʿbah. What protects is believing the news before it arrives.

passages.title: Creation in truth and the Day of Decision
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** The ayah just before this one pointed back at a vanished people — "Are they better, or the people of Tubbaʿ?" (44:37) — and now the sūrah lifts its gaze from history to the whole universe and asks the deepest question of all: why does any of this exist? Ayat 38–39 answer that the heavens and the earth were not made in play but *with true purpose*; ayat 40–42 then draw the necessary conclusion — a world made with purpose must end in a reckoning, on a Day when every human support gives way and nothing remains but the mercy of Allah.

What holds these five ayat together is a single chain of reasoning. Purpose in creation (38–39) requires a Day of Decision (40); a Day of Decision means each soul stands alone (41); and standing alone means salvation can only be a gift, not a favour called in (42).

## Where we have just come from

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *Tubbaʿ* is not the name of a particular individual but is said to be the royal title of the kings of Himyar in Yemen. The kings of Yemen were known by this title when they held sway over Himyar, Arabia, Syria, ʿIraq and parts of Africa for a long time, with the western part of Yemen as their capital — hence the plural *Tabābiʿah*, and the kings are called the Tabābiʿah of Yemen. Which of them is meant here is not clear, but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Kathir's research and conclusion to be the most plausible: that the Tubbaʿ intended is Tubbaʿ Awsat (the "Middle Tubbaʿ"), whose name was Asʿad Abū Kurayb ibn Maʿdīkarab al-Yamanī. He ruled at least seven hundred years before the advent of the Prophet ﷺ, ruled the longest of the Himyarī kings, and went on a journey of conquest, annexing many regions until he reached Samarqand.

According to the narration of Muhammad ibn Isḥāq, related in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, on one of those campaigns he passed by the area of Madinah and intended to attack it. Its inhabitants took the attitude that by day they resisted his attacks and by night they entertained him — until he felt embarrassed and abandoned the intention of fighting. During this period two Jewish rabbis warned him that this was the place of migration of the Final Prophet of Allah ﷺ, and that he would never be able to prevail over that city. He was persuaded, left Madinah, and went away with the two rabbis to Yemen. They invited him to embrace the Mosaic religion and he accepted it, and his people were influenced by him and embraced it too. After his death, however, they went astray and reverted to idolatry and fire-worship, and this brought down on them the divine wrath, the details of which are available in Sūrah Sabaʼ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the point out precisely: this incident shows that the Tubbaʿ mentioned here had himself embraced Islam, while his people later went astray — and on both occasions the Qurʼān makes reference to *the people of Tubbaʿ*, not to Tubbaʿ himself. This is supported by the narratives of Sayyidnā Sahl ibn Saʿd and Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them), recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Imam Ahmad, Ṭabarānī and others, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not revile Tubbaʿ, because he had embraced Islam."

So the warning is not aimed at a man who submitted but at a people who inherited faith and then let it go. And with that, the argument widens from one ruined nation to the entire cosmos.

## Ayah 38 — "not as players"

*Wa mā khalaqnā s-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa wa mā baynahumā lāʿibīn.* "We did not create the heavens and the earth and everything between them as players."

Ibn Kathir titles this section *This World was created for a Wisdom*, and states the meaning directly: here Allah tells us of His justice, and that He is far above mere play, folly and falsehood. The denial is about Him — He was not at play when He made this.

This is why the ayah belongs in a passage about judgement. If creation were play, the moral shape of a life would be decoration. Ibn Kathir gathers two other places where the Qurʼān makes the same move, and reading them beside this one shows how consistently the point is pressed:

> "And We created not the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose! That is the consideration of those who disbelieve! Then woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire!" (38:27)

Note what that ayah does: it names purposelessness as *the disbelievers' own estimate* of reality, and then attaches the Fire to it. To think the world is without purpose is not treated as a neutral opinion; the ayah itself ties a warning to it.

> "Did you think that We had created you in play, and that you would not be brought back to Us? So Exalted be Allah, the True King: lā ilāha illā Huwa, the Lord of the Supreme Throne!" (23:115–116)

Here the two halves are welded together — *created in play* and *not brought back to Us* are one thought. Deny the return and you have said the creation was a game. And the response is not an argument but an exaltation: **fa-taʿālā Allāh** — far exalted is Allah above such a thought.

## Ayah 39 — "not except with true purpose"

*Mā khalaqnāhumā illā bi-l-ḥaqq wa lākinna aktharahum lā yaʿlamūn.* "We did not create them but with true purpose, yet most of them do not know."

Ayah 38 clears the ground by denial; ayah 39 builds on it by affirmation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: every wise and thinking person should realise that there is a purpose and objective for creating this universe. The heavens and the earth and everything created in them manifest many realities, and it lists four:

**1. The manifestation of divine power.** What exists is itself a display of the power that brought it about.

**2. The possibility of the Hereafter.** Obviously, the Supreme Creator who drew out such huge bodies from the realm of non-existence into the realm of existence surely has the power to destroy them and re-create them. The argument runs from what we can already see to what we are asked to believe.

**3. The need for retribution — reward and punishment.** This is the hinge of the whole passage. If there is no retribution in the Hereafter, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the very existence of the universe would be rendered purposeless, or its purpose would be defeated — because then "the outcome of both good and bad will necessarily be the same," and that is far from divine wisdom. The wisdom underlying the creation of the universe is to make it *dār al-imtiḥān*, the domain of test and trial, while the Hereafter is the domain of reward and punishment. Take away the second and the first collapses.

**4. Urging thinking people to obedience and gratitude.** The whole universe was granted to man as Allah's great blessing, and these ayat urge the thinking person to obey Allah and to thank Him for it.

**"Yet most of them do not know."** The ayah does not say most of them *cannot* know. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole reflection as what "every wise and thinking person should realise" — putting the failure not in the evidence but in the failure to stop and think about it.

## Ayah 40 — the appointed time

*Inna yawma-l-faṣli mīqātuhum ajmaʿīn.* "Verily, the Day of Judgement is the time appointed for all of them."

Ibn Kathir identifies the Day plainly: this is the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will judge between all creatures, and He will punish the disbelievers and reward the believers. Every dispute this world leaves unsettled is settled there, and the settling is a judgement between all creatures — not a category left open.

And on *mīqātuhum ajmaʿīn* — "the time appointed for all of them" — Ibn Kathir adds: it means He will gather all of them, the first and the last of them. No generation is skipped. No one dies too early or too late to be included. The proud kings of the earlier passage and every soul after them are gathered to the same appointment.

## Ayah 41 — the day the ties go slack

*Yawma lā yughnī mawlan ʿan mawlan shayʼan wa lā hum yunṣarūn.* "The Day when a near relative cannot avail a near relative in aught, and no help can they receive."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact and unsparing: it means no relative will be able to help another relative. Read the ayah slowly and it removes the safety net a human being most instinctively relies on — the family that would always cover for you.

Ibn Kathir sets two ayat beside it, and together they cover both kinds of bond — blood and affection:

> "Then, when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask of one another." (23:101)

Kinship does not merely fail to help; as a working claim on another person, it is gone.

> "And no friend will ask a friend about his condition — though they shall be made to see one another." (70:10–11)

This is the more haunting of the two, and Ibn Kathir draws out precisely why: it means he will not ask his brother about how he is, **even though he can see him with his own eyes**. They are not separated by distance. He is right there, in view — and no one asks.

**"And no help can they receive."** Ibn Kathir closes the last door: no relative will help another, and no help will come to him from outside. Not from within the family, not from beyond it.

## Ayah 42 — except whom Allah has mercy upon

*Illā man raḥima-llāh. Innahu Huwa-l-ʿAzīzu-r-Raḥīm.* "Except him on whom Allah has mercy. Verily, He is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

Everything the passage has been closing off was closed off for this. After the exhaustive denial — no kin, no friend, no help from outside — one exception is named, and it is not a category of person who managed better. It is an act of Allah. Ibn Kathir states it exactly: nothing will be of any avail that Day except the mercy of Allah towards His creation.

That is why the ayah seals with two names held together, and Ibn Kathir reads them together: **He is the Almighty, with immense mercy.**

Pair them and the tone of the whole passage settles. Might named on its own would leave the ayah as pure dread. Mercy named on its own could be mistaken for wishful thinking. But the ayah gives both of Allah at once, in one breath, and it is on the mercy of the All-Mighty that the exception rests.

## Living it

**Take the purpose of the world seriously.** Ayat 38–39 are not abstract theology. If Allah is far above mere play, folly and falsehood in what He made, then a life lived as play is out of step with reality itself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase is the one to carry: this world is *dār al-imtiḥān*, the domain of test and trial, and the Hereafter is the domain of reward and punishment. That reframes an ordinary day — the difficulty is part of the test.

**Look at creation and let it land.** "Most of them do not know" sits right beside Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's call to what "every wise and thinking person should realise," and the reflection it prescribes ends in two actions: obeying Allah, and thanking Him for having granted man this entire creation as His great blessing. Looking up and thinking is worship when it lands there.

**Build the one relationship that will still be standing.** Ayah 41 is not a reason to love family less — it is a reason not to *bank* on them. Ibn Kathir's image of a man who can see his own brother with his own eyes and still does not ask after him should quietly rearrange our priorities.

**Ask for the exception.** Since Ibn Kathir says nothing will be of any avail that Day except the mercy of Allah towards His creation, mercy should be the thing we ask for most. Deeds matter — this whole passage exists to say that outcomes are not all the same — but we walk in, if we walk in, under *illā man raḥima-llāh*. That is not a reason to relax; it is a reason to keep asking the One who is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.

passages.title: The tree of Zaqqum and hellfire's torment
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These eight ayat form a single scene: a meal, an arrest, and a sentence spoken aloud. Ibn Kathir titles the passage "The Condition of the Idolators and Their Punishment on the Day of Resurrection," and opens by saying that "Allah tells us how He will punish the disbelievers who deny the meeting with Him."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this follows the style of the Qur'an: in these verses Allah describes Hell and the way the unbelievers will be punished, and Paradise and the way the believers will be rewarded.

## The tree that is served as food (43–44)

**"Surely ˹the fruit of˺ the tree of Zaqqūm will be the food of the evildoer."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that the necessary information about the reality of zaqqūm has already been given in Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt, and refers the reader back to (37:64–65) rather than repeating it here.

**Who is "al-athīm"?** Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as "those who sinned by their words and in deeds. These are the disbelievers." Both the tongue and the limbs are named.

Ibn Kathir then reports that **more than one commentator stated that this referred to Abu Jahl** — and adds a caution worth learning from: "undoubtedly he is included among those referred to in this Ayah, but it is not specifically about him." A named individual may be a clear instance of a verse without the verse shrinking down to him. The warning stands for everyone whose words and deeds are like his.

**The reciter who slipped.** Ibn Jarir recorded that Abu ad-Dardā', may Allah be pleased with him, was reciting this ayah to a man — *ṭaʿām al-athīm*, "the food of the evildoer." The man said it back as **"the food of the orphan."** Abu ad-Dardā' did not simply repeat the same syllables at him. He said: **"Say, the tree of Zaqqūm is the food of the evildoer,"** giving him a plainer word for the wrongdoer that he could manage.

Two things are in that exchange. One misreading turns a verse about the wicked into a verse about the child who most deserves our care — the meaning is not merely blurred, it is reversed. And a Companion's instinct was to make sure the man did not walk away carrying the wrong sense. Recite it right; and know what it says.

Ibn Kathir adds his own explanatory note on the word *ṭaʿām*, "food": **he will not have any other food apart from that.** Food is what sustains. Here the only thing on offer is the thing that destroys.

**Mujahid's measure.** Mujahid said: **"If a drop of it were to fall on the earth, it would corrupt the living of all the people of earth."** One drop — not a branch, not a fruit — and the livelihood of everyone on earth is spoiled. Ibn Kathir notes that a similar *marfūʿ* report — a report traced back to the Prophet ﷺ — has been narrated earlier, though he does not restate its wording here. Hold the image: this is what the disbeliever is served as a *meal*.

## When is it served? A genuine difference among the scholars

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a question the passage itself provokes, and it is worth following because it shows careful scholars reasoning in the open.

Read the sequence plainly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that here the Qur'an **apparently indicates that the infidels will be given zaqqūm to eat even before they enter Hell**, because the verse says that after being fed with zaqqūm they will be seized by the keepers of Hell and dragged into the middle of the blazing fire. According to some commentators, this is the meaning of Allah's words in Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah, *"This will be their entertainment on the Day of Requital"* (56:56). They argue from the word itself: **nuzul** ("entertainment") originally refers to the starter food and provision served to guests to make them feel welcome, before the main course; the main course served later on is called *ḍiyāfah* or *maʾdubah*.

But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not close the case there. It notes that **the wordings of the Qur'an do carry the possibility that the feeding of zaqqūm could be after the entry into Hell**, in which case *nuzul* would refer, by extension, to the main course of meals and provisions served. On that reading, the verse about dragging the dweller of Hell towards the middle of the blazing fire means he would already be in Hell, and after being fed zaqqūm he is dragged toward the middle "to expose him to a greater degree of disgrace and torture."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends where a scholar should end on a matter of the unseen: **"Allah knows best!"** (condensed there from Bayān-ul-Qurʼān). Both readings honour the words. What both agree on is the substance — the food, the Fire, and the humiliation.

## What boils inside them (45–46)

**"Like molten metal, it will boil in the bellies, like the boiling of hot water."**

The Arabic word is **al-muhl**. Ibn Kathir explains it as **"like the dregs of oil"** — the thick sediment at the bottom of the vessel; hence some renderings give "boiling oil" and others "molten metal."

And why does it boil inside them? Ibn Kathir answers briefly: **"because of its heat and rancidity."** The food itself carries the punishment within it, and continues to work after it is swallowed.

Note where the verse places it: *fi'l-buṭūn*, "in the bellies" — inside the body. Ayah 46 then supplies the comparison that makes it graspable: *like the boiling of scalding water*.

## The arrest (47–48)

Now the register changes. Ayat 43–46 were description; ayah 47 is a **command**:

**"˹It will be said,˺ 'Seize them and drag them into the depths… Then pour over their heads the torment of boiling water.'"** Ibn Kathir's rendering runs: *"Seize him and drag him into the midst of blazing Fire, then pour over his head the torment of boiling water."*

**"Seize him"** — *khudhūhu*. Ibn Kathir says plainly: this means the disbeliever. And he passes on a report that when Allah says to the keepers of Hell, "Seize him," **seventy thousand of them will rush to seize him.**

**"and drag him"** — *fa-ʿtilūhu*. Ibn Kathir explains it as **dragging him by pulling him and pushing him on his back**; Mujahid's gloss is compressed to the bone: **"take him and push him."** He is not walked; he is hauled.

**"into the midst"** — *ilā sawāʾ al-jaḥīm*. Ibn Kathir: **"into the middle of it."** Not the edge. The centre.

**Then the boiling water** (48). Ibn Kathir sets this alongside Allah's words in Sūrah al-Ḥajj: *"boiling water will be poured down over their heads. With it will melt what is within their bellies, as well as (their) skins"* (22:19–20). And he relates: **the angel will strike him with a hooked rod of iron and split his head open, then he will pour boiling water over his head; it will go down through his body, melting through his stomach and intestines, until it goes through his heels.**

Ibn Kathir does not narrate this coolly. He breaks off with a prayer — **"may Allah protect us from that."** That is the correct posture for a reader too. This is not material for the imagination to enjoy; it is material for *duʿāʾ* — calling on Allah, asking Him directly. The right response to reading it is to ask Allah to shield you from it.

## The mocking title (49)

**"Taste this. You mighty, noble one!"** — *dhuq innaka anta al-ʿazīz al-karīm.*

Ibn Kathir states who speaks and why: **the keepers of Hell will say that to him by way of ridicule and rebuke.** His rendering of the words makes the sting explicit — *you were (pretending to be) the mighty, the generous.* The description is handed back to the man who once claimed it.

Ad-Daḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, the whole point in a few words: **"This means, you are neither mighty nor generous."**

And note the imperative that opens the ayah: **"Taste."** The verb reaches back to ayat 43–44, to the food he has been given.

## "This is what you used to doubt" (50)

**"This is truly what you ˹all˺ used to doubt."**

The sentence lands on the word for doubt — *tamtarūn*. And notice how wide the address becomes: ayah 49 speaks to a single figure — *taste, you mighty, noble one* — while ayah 50 says "what you *all* used to doubt." That fits exactly what Ibn Kathir said at ayah 44: Abu Jahl is included, but the verse is not specifically about him.

Ibn Kathir places this beside the parallel in Sūrah aṭ-Ṭūr: *"The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing. This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see?"* (52:13–15). Both passages do the same thing: they take the denial the person once voiced and hold it up against the reality now in front of him.

## What the passage asks of us

**Turn the description into duʿāʾ — supplication.** Ibn Kathir models it: he narrates the boiling water melting through the body and immediately says, *may Allah protect us from that.* When these ayat pass in your recitation or in ṣalāh, do not read past them flatly. Ask for protection.

**Weigh what you are proud of.** Ayah 49 is aimed at the one who was addressed as *al-ʿazīz al-karīm*, "the mighty, the generous" — a description Ibn Kathir says he was only pretending to. Ibn ʿAbbās's verdict on it, once the truth is uncovered, is that he was **neither mighty nor generous**. That is worth measuring your own self-image against.

**Take doubt seriously.** The passage ends by naming what these people did with their minds: they doubted. Ibn Kathir opened his commentary on the passage with the same framing — these are the ones "who deny the meeting with Him." Unsettled conviction is not a harmless private condition; it shapes a whole life.

**And guard the meaning when you recite.** Abu ad-Dardā', may Allah be pleased with him, would not let a man walk away saying "the food of the orphan" in place of "the food of the evildoer." Recite carefully, and know what the words mean.

passages.title: The righteous in gardens and security
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat close Sūrah ad-Dukhān with a portrait of the people of taqwā in Paradise, drawn as the exact opposite of the picture of the doomed that came just before. And one note keeps sounding through it: **security**. Ibn Kathir's renderings alone carry it three times — a "place of security," fruit called for "in peace and security," a place "free from fear" as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has it. Not merely pleasure, but pleasure that can never be lost.

## Why this passage sits exactly here

Ibn Kathir points out the pattern plainly: when Allah describes the state of the doomed, He follows that with a description of the life of the blessed. And it is for this reason, he says, that the Qur'an is called *al-Mathānī* — the oft-repeated.

You can hear that pairing in ayah 52. The people before them had the tree of Zaqqūm and boiling water; these have **"gardens and springs."** Ibn Kathir says this is in direct contrast to the state of the doomed. Bitter tree against green garden, scalding drink against flowing spring. The Qur'an does not simply switch subjects — it answers the previous image point for point.

## The six things a human being needs

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a beautifully practical key to the passage. It observes that almost all sorts of blessings have been referred to in these verses, because the following are generally the human needs:

1. a fine dwelling
2. fine clothing
3. the best life-partner
4. the best food
5. the satisfaction that these blessings will remain available
6. assurance of total security from grief and affliction

And it says that in these verses **all six kinds of blessings** for the inmates of Paradise have been mentioned. That is not a random heap of delights. It is a complete human life, rebuilt with every defect removed. Then it turns to the first of the six — the dwelling — and that is where we should begin too.

## Ayah 51 — "a secure place"

The passage opens: *inna al-muttaqīna fī maqāmin amīn.* Ibn Kathir glosses **al-muttaqīn** as those who fear Allah and are dutiful towards Him *in this world* — taqwā is a description of how a person lived here, before it becomes a description of where they arrive there.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the place as one **"free from fear,"** and comments that the best human dwelling is the one that is secure from all kinds of dangers. That is a shrewd observation about ourselves: a palace under threat is not a home. What ruins a beautiful house is not that it lacks beauty but that it can be lost.

Ibn Kathir unfolds what they are safe *from*, and the list is worth reading slowly. In Paradise they will be safe:

- from death, and from the fear of ever leaving it
- from every kind of worry, grief, terror and exhaustion
- from the Shayṭān and his wiles
- from all other troubles and disasters

Notice how much of that describes not physical harm but the inner weather of a human life — the low hum of anxiety, the tiredness, the grief we carry, the whispering that pulls us off course. The first blessing named in Paradise is the removal of the very things that make even our happiest days here feel provisional.

## Ayah 53 — silk, and the geometry of a gathering

**Sundus** and **istabraq**: both words refer to silk. Ibn Kathir explains *sundus* as the finest of silk — the sort used for shirts and the like — and *istabraq* as silk woven with shiny threads, like a splendid garment which is worn over regular clothes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it more simply: *sundus* is fine silk, *istabraq* is thick silk. Put the two glosses together and you get the picture of a full outfit: the soft inner garment and the lustrous robe over it. Even in the wardrobe of Paradise there is layering, taste, and honour — clothing is not just covering, it is dignity.

Then one word changes the whole scene: **mutaqābilīn**, "facing one another." Ibn Kathir explains it as sitting on thrones where none of them will sit with his back to anyone else.

Stop on that. Of all the details Allah could have mentioned about the seating, He mentions that nobody's back is turned. A turned back is the posture of a slight, a coldness, a falling-out. In Paradise that posture simply does not exist. Every face is toward every other face. The blessing here is *social*: a gathering with no exclusion in it, no cliques, no one left on the edge of the circle. Much of the misery of this world is people arranged badly toward one another; ayah 53 quietly fixes that.

## Ayah 54 — "And We shall pair them with ḥūr ʿīn"

Ibn Kathir treats this as an addition to what the believers already have: this, he says, will be a gift **in addition to** the beautiful wives given to them. He then draws on Sūrah ar-Raḥmān to describe the ḥūr: that no man or jinn has touched them before (55:56), that in beauty *"they are like rubies and Marjān"* (55:58) — and he closes the group of citations with a verse that frames the whole passage: *"Is there any reward for good other than good?"* (55:60). That verse is doing real work here. Everything in these ayat stands as the answer to a single question: what does *iḥsān* — excellence, doing good beautifully — deserve? Only *iḥsān*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the verb **zawwajnā**. The word *tazwīj*, it explains, originally means "to make one person partner of another"; later on it came to be used abundantly in the sense of "marrying." Both senses are live here, and the verse is read accordingly:

- **Taken in the later sense** — the people of Paradise will be married, technically, to the ḥūr ʿīn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the apparent sense of ayah 54, and it answers the obvious question itself: although the inmates of Paradise will not be legally obligated to observe the precepts of the Sharīʿah, the purpose of the marriage there will be **to honour them** — so this should not raise any objection.
- **Taken in the original sense** — of simply being made partners — the ḥūr ʿīn are given as life-partners, granted to them as a gift, with no need for a contract of marriage as is done in this world.

Either way, the note Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sounds is *honour*. This is not merely appetite satisfied; it is a person being dignified by their Lord.

## Ayah 55 — fruit, and the guarantee attached to it

*"They will call therein for every kind of fruit"* — and then, once again, the sentence does not end without a guarantee: **in peace and security**.

Ibn Kathir spells out what that security means here: whatever kinds of fruit they ask for will be brought to them, and they will have the security of knowing that **this supply will never come to an end or be withheld**; these fruits will be brought to them whenever they want.

Two anxieties are answered at once — that the good thing will run out, and that it will be refused. Every pleasure in this life is shadowed by one or the other. In ayah 55 both shadows are gone. And notice that the passage has now used the language of security twice, at its opening and here in its middle: it is the thread the whole description is strung on.

## Ayah 56 — "except the first death"

*"They will never taste death therein except the first death."*

The grammar here is unusual, and Ibn Kathir addresses it directly: **this is an exception which reinforces the negation.** In other words, the exception is not carving out some death that still occurs in Paradise — it is a construction that strengthens the "never." The meaning, he says plainly, is that they will never taste death there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way: they shall suffer no death other than the first death, the one they had encountered at the end of their lives in this world.

For this ayah Ibn Kathir brings the ḥadīth reported in the **Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: death will be brought forth in the image of a fine ram, made to stand between Paradise and Hell, and then slaughtered. Then it will be said: *"O people of Paradise, it is eternal, no more death; and O people of Hell, it is eternal, no more death."* (He notes the ḥadīth was already quoted in his discussion of Sūrah Maryam.)

He also cites a report from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah — recorded by **Muslim** — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said it will be said to the people of Paradise: *"It is granted to you that you will be healthy and will never fall ill, you will live and never die, you will enjoy a life of luxury and will never be miserable, you will be youthful and will never grow old."* Four sentences, four of the deepest fears of a human body — sickness, death, hardship, ageing — each cancelled.

And Ibn Kathir reports from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever has taqwā of Allah will enter Paradise and enjoy a life of luxury and never be miserable; he will live therein and never die, his clothes will never wear out and his youth will never fade.

**The same fact, felt in opposite directions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking observation on this ayah. The dwellers of Hell, too, will suffer only one death, at the end of their lives in this world. But that single fact lands on the two groups in completely opposite ways. The people of Hell will suffer a greater degree of torture when they know that they will remain alive in that miserable state of punishment. For the people of Paradise, the thought that Allah has saved them from the torment of Hell, that the gardens are eternal, that they will enjoy the delights of Paradise forever and that its blessings will never cease or be taken away — that thought *enhances* the degree of their happiness, never to diminish. Permanence is not neutral. It multiplies whatever it is attached to.

The second half of ayah 56 completes the pair: *"and He will save them from the torment of the blazing Fire."* Ibn Kathir explains that along with this great and eternal blessing, He will also have saved them from the agonising torment in the depths of Hell — **so they will have achieved their desired aim and avoided the thing they feared.** That is the whole of a believer's hope in one sentence: to get what you longed for and escape what you dreaded.

## Ayah 57 — the word that reframes everything

*Faḍlan min rabbik* — **"as a bounty from your Lord."**

After six ayat of reward, Allah closes with a correction to how we might have been reading them. Ibn Kathir's gloss is short: that will be from His bounty and kindness towards them. Not a wage collected. A gift given.

He supports it with the ḥadīth reported in the **Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Work and strive hard, and know that no one will enter Paradise by virtue of his deeds."* They said, "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said: *"Not even me, unless Allah showers me with His mercy and grace."*

Hold that against ayah 57 and the balance of the passage becomes clear. **"Work and strive hard"** — deeds are commanded, seriously and urgently. **"No one will enter Paradise by virtue of his deeds"** — but no amount of deeds *purchases* what has just been described. Ayah 51 begins with *al-muttaqīn*, so effort is real and required; ayah 57 ends with *faḍlan*, so the effort is never the price. And the ḥadīth closes the door on any exception: not even the best of creation ﷺ enters except by the mercy and grace of Allah.

Then the closing verdict: *dhālika huwa al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm* — "that will be the supreme success." The Qur'an lets that word stand alone. Whatever else in this life gets called success, this alone receives the definite verdict.

## Living it

Read the passage backwards and it becomes a way of living forwards.

- **Taqwā is the entry condition, not a personality type.** Ibn Kathir defines the *muttaqīn* simply as those who fear Allah and are dutiful towards Him in this world. The report from Abū Hurayrah puts it as a plain conditional: whoever has taqwā of Allah enters Paradise. It is available.
- **Strive without invoicing.** "Work and strive hard" and "no one enters by his deeds" are not in tension; holding both together is what keeps a believer from despair on the one hand and self-satisfaction on the other.
- **Name what you actually want.** The six needs Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists — home, clothing, companionship, food, the certainty that these remain, and total security from grief and affliction — are the same six most of us spend our lives chasing here, in forms that break. The passage does not tell you to stop wanting them. It tells you where they are kept intact.
- **Watch the turned back.** Of everything in ayah 53, the detail that costs us nothing to imitate today is *mutaqābilīn* — a gathering in which nobody is seated with his back to anyone else.

passages.title: The Quran made easy; now wait
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close Sūrah ad-Dukhān. After a long stretch of warning and then a long stretch of promise, Allah turns to His Messenger ﷺ and says two things: this Qur'an has been made easy in your tongue so that people may remember — and, since some of them still refuse it, wait; they are waiting too. Both ayat are addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: ayah 58 tells him what he has been given, ayah 59 tells him what to do while people decide what to do with it.

## Where the passage lands

Ibn Kathir treats ayat 51–59 as one continuous stretch, and the placement matters. The ayat just before described the people of taqwā — those who fear Allah and are dutiful towards Him in this world — in a place of security: gardens and springs, the finest silk, thrones where none of them sits with his back to anyone else, every kind of fruit called for in peace and security, and no death after the first death.

Ibn Kathir notes the deliberate design of this. When Allah describes the state of the doomed, He follows it with a description of the life of the blessed. For this reason, he says, the Qur'an is called *al-Mathānī* — the oft-repeated. The gardens and springs, he points out, stand in direct contrast to the state of the doomed, who will have the tree of Zaqqūm and boiling water.

Then ayah 57 caps the scene: **"As a bounty from your Lord! That will be the supreme success."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and decisive — that will be from His bounty and kindness towards them. And he brings here the report from the Two Sahihs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Work and strive hard, and know that no one will enter Paradise by virtue of his deeds."* They said, "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said, *"Not even me, unless Allah showers me with His mercy and grace."* Effort is commanded there and excused for nobody; but the door is opened by mercy, not purchased by works.

So when ayah 58 says "We have made this easy in your tongue", the "this" arrives already loaded. Everything just described — the two destinations, the supreme success — is what has been made accessible.

## "We have made this easy in your tongue"

**فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَاهُ بِلِسَانِكَ** — *fa-innamā yassarnāhu bi-lisānik.*

Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is worth reading slowly: *"We have made this Qur'an, which We have sent down, easy, plain and clear, in your language which is the most eloquent, clear and beautiful of all languages."*

Three words carry the ease — **easy**, **plain**, **clear**. To say Allah made it easy is not to say He made it shallow; it is to say the message is not obscure. It does not need a priestly caste to unlock it. Its warnings warn in words people can follow. And the language it came in is, in Ibn Kathir's description, the most eloquent, clear and beautiful of all languages — so the ease is not a lowering of the Book but a quality of it.

Notice too where the phrase places the Book: **in your tongue**, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself. The revelation is bound to his recitation.

## "In order that they may remember"

**لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ** — *la'allahum yatadhakkarūn.*

Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: *"in order that they may understand and know."* That gloss matters, because it stops us at the right place. Ease is not the goal. Ease is the means; the goal is that a human being should actually take the thing in — understand it, know it.

Notice the direction of the sentence. Allah speaks to the Prophet ﷺ in the second person — *your* tongue — but the purpose clause is about *them*, the listeners. The Book was eased for the Messenger's ﷺ recitation for the sake of the people who would hear it. Revelation is not given as a private possession. It is given to be passed on.

## Plain, and still refused

Here the passage turns, and this is the hinge between the two ayat. Ibn Kathir puts it starkly: *"Despite the fact that it is so plain and clear, there are still people who disbelieve, who stubbornly go against it."*

That one sentence explains why ayah 59 exists at all. If the message were confusing, rejection would be a comprehension problem, and the cure would be more explanation. But the message has been made easy, plain and clear — so rejection, in Ibn Kathir's reading, is stubbornness rather than a failure of the message.

And so, he says, Allah speaks to His Messenger ﷺ here doing three things at once: **consoling him**, **promising him victory**, and **warning those who reject him that they will be destroyed.** Anyone who has ever explained something true, clearly, to someone who did not want it, stands in the shadow of that consolation.

## "Wait then; verily, they too are waiting"

**فَٱرْتَقِبْ إِنَّهُم مُّرْتَقِبُونَ** — *fa-rtaqib innahum murtaqibūn.*

The ayah sets the same act on both sides of the line: you wait — and they, too, are waiting. But the two waitings are not the same waiting, and that is the whole force of it. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *"they will come to know who will be victorious and whose word will prevail in this world and in the Hereafter. For victory will be for you, O Muhammad, and for your brothers among the Prophets and Messengers, and for the believers who followed you."* One side waits for a promise it has been given. The other side waits for an outcome it has merely assumed. Only one of them has been told how it ends.

Ibn Kathir supports this by citing Allah's words elsewhere:

- **"Allah has decreed: Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious."** (58:21)
- **"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth — the Day when their excuses will be of no profit to wrongdoers. Theirs will be the curse, and theirs will be the evil abode."** (40:51–52)

Two things stand out in those citations. First, the victory promised is **in this world's life and on the Day** the witnesses stand forth — not deferred entirely to the Hereafter, and not confined to this life either. Second, on Ibn Kathir's reading the promise reaches beyond the Prophet ﷺ himself: to his brothers among the Prophets and Messengers, and to *the believers who followed him*. The waiting of ayah 59 is therefore not his alone. Anyone holding a clear message in front of people who will not have it is included in that "wait" — and in that promise.

## Living it

**Take the ease seriously.** Allah says He made this Book easy, plain and clear. That is an invitation, and it is also a removal of excuses. A Book described by its Author as eased is meant to be received — not treated as sound without sense. Ibn Kathir's gloss on *yatadhakkarūn* — that they may understand and know — sets the bar: not merely hearing it, but taking its meaning in.

**Do not measure the truth by how people receive it.** The passage explicitly separates the two. Clarity was achieved; rejection happened anyway. If you have conveyed something well and it was refused, ayah 58 tells you the fault is not necessarily in the conveying.

**Wait as one who has been promised, not as one who is anxious.** *Irtaqib* is a command, not a mood — a watching grounded in Allah's own decree that He and His Messengers will prevail. That is different from passivity, and it is the opposite of despair.

**Remember whose bounty it is.** The Paradise described just before this passage is called, in ayah 57, a bounty from your Lord — and in the hadith Ibn Kathir brings from the Two Sahihs, even the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said he would not enter it unless Allah showers him with His mercy and grace. Strive hard, and lean on His mercy. Both together.

## The last word of the sūrah

It is worth pausing on how Sūrah ad-Dukhān ends. A sūrah that set the tree of Zaqqūm and boiling water against gardens, springs, silk and security does not close on either scene. It closes on a single imperative to the Prophet ﷺ: **wait.** The scenes have been shown; the message has been made easy, plain and clear in his own tongue; what remains is time, and Allah's promise about how time ends.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on this sūrah with the words that all praise and thanks are due to Allah, and in Him is all strength and protection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes simply with *Alhamdulillāh*.
